a: his anointed
p: The only foreigner the Bible calls the LORD's 'anointed', the word that later meant 'messiah'.
b: Mashiach, 'anointed one', is the title of Israel's kings ("the LORD's anointed", 1 Samuel 24:6) and of priests (Leviticus 4:3). Here it is given to a Persian king who had never been anointed with oil and did not know the LORD (45:4–5). The word means a ruler chosen and empowered by God for a task, not yet the later sense 'the Messiah', the coming king of David's line (Daniel 9:25 stands between the two uses). The Greek has tō christō mou, 'my christ', the word from which 'Christ' comes. Jewish and Christian readers alike have found it startling: the LORD uses a pagan emperor to free his people, so that the nations may know there is no other God (45:6).
r: 44:28; 1 Samuel 24:6; Leviticus 4:3; Psalm 2:2; Daniel 9:25; 2 Chronicles 36:22–23; Ezra 1:1–2

a: to Cyrus
t: Cyrus the Great and his cylinder
p: Cyrus II took Babylon in 539 BC; his own clay cylinder uses language much like this verse.
b: Cyrus II of Persia (ruled 559–530 BC) conquered Media (about 550), Lydia with its capital Sardis (about 547) and Babylon (October 539). The Nabonidus Chronicle says his army entered Babylon without a battle. The Cyrus Cylinder, a Babylonian clay barrel inscription found in 1879 and now in the British Museum, says that Marduk, Babylon's god, searched for a righteous king, "took under his hand Cyrus, king of the city of Anshan, and called him by his name", and that Cyrus returned displaced peoples and their gods to their homes. The likeness to 45:1–4 (the hand taken, the name called) is striking. Historians such as Amélie Kuhrt warn that the cylinder is royal propaganda written for Babylon, not a general charter of religious freedom; it does not mention Judah.

a: whose right hand I have gripped
t: Named in advance, or named in his own day?
p: How Cyrus could be named here is the book's central authorship question; see the note at 44:28.
b: Isaiah of Jerusalem lived about 740–700 BC; Cyrus rose about 550. The traditional view, held by many Jewish and Christian scholars (Oswalt, Motyer), is that God revealed the name in advance, and that this is the point of the passage: the LORD alone announces events before they happen (45:21; 46:10; 48:3–5). Josephus says Cyrus himself read Isaiah's prophecy and was moved by it (Antiquities 11.5–6). The critical view, the consensus since the 1800s, is that chapters 40–55 come from a prophet among the exiles about 545–539 BC, who saw Cyrus advancing and declared him the LORD's chosen instrument; his claim that God had foretold it rests on earlier prophecies now fulfilled (48:3). Both readings take the passage as a claim about God's control of history. The full case for each is given in the book's opening pages and at 44:28.

a: The LORD says this to his anointed
p: An early Christian letter reads the Greek 'to Cyrus' as 'to the Lord', making the verse speak of Christ.
b: In Greek the name Cyrus (Kyrō) differs from 'Lord' (kyriō) by one letter. The Letter of Barnabas, an early Christian writing (about AD 100–130), quotes the verse as "The Lord said to Christ, my Lord, whose right hand I have held" (Barnabas 12:11), and uses it as a prophecy of Jesus beside Psalm 110:1. A later corrector of Codex Sinaiticus, the manuscript that preserves Barnabas, changed it back to 'Cyrus'. No manuscript of Isaiah reads 'Lord' here; the reading is a Christian interpretation, not Isaiah's text.

a: doors of bronze
p: Herodotus says Babylon's wall had a hundred gates, all of bronze.
b: The Greek historian Herodotus, writing about a century after Cyrus, says the wall of Babylon had "a hundred gates, all of bronze, with bronze posts and lintels" (Histories 1.179). Babylonian building inscriptions of Nebuchadnezzar also boast of gates covered with bronze. The picture of the LORD smashing the doors and bars ahead of Cyrus fits a king who in fact took the city with almost no fighting (Nabonidus Chronicle). Herodotus also tells that Cyrus entered by diverting the Euphrates, a story many historians doubt.

a: treasures kept in the dark
p: Cyrus's conquests made him master of the richest treasuries of the age.
b: When Cyrus took Sardis about 547 BC he captured the treasury of Croesus, king of Lydia, proverbial for his wealth (Herodotus, Histories 1.84–88). Babylon's temple stores followed in 539. 'Treasures of darkness' are riches stored in sealed rooms or buried. The purpose clause is the point: the wealth is given "so that you will know that I am the LORD", though Cyrus credited Marduk on his own cylinder.

a: I gave you a title of honor
p: The verb means to give someone a title or a flattering name.
b: 'Akhannekha comes from kanah, 'give a title, call by an honorable name' (Job 32:21–22). The titles in view are probably 'my shepherd' (44:28) and 'his anointed' (45:1). The repeated "though you did not know me" (45:4, 5) is the surprise of the passage: God's choice of Cyrus does not depend on Cyrus knowing or worshiping the LORD.

a: I will fasten your belt on you
p: God loosens the belts of kings (45:1) and fastens Cyrus's belt: he disarms some and arms another.
b: To 'gird' a man was to tie on the belt that held his sword and tucked up his robe for action (1 Kings 20:11; Psalm 18:39). To loosen it was to disarm him. The two halves of the image frame 45:1–5: the kings' belts come undone, Cyrus is dressed for war, and the one doing both is the LORD.

a: there is no one else
p: The Bible's plainest statements that the LORD alone is God are in Isaiah 43–46.
b: The phrase 'en 'od, 'there is no more, no other', comes again and again in these chapters (45:5, 6, 14, 18, 21, 22; 46:9), with 'apart from me there is no God'. It continues Deuteronomy's creed (Deuteronomy 4:35, 39; 32:39) and goes further: the other gods are not rivals but nothing at all (44:9–20; 46:1–7). Scholars often call Isaiah 40–55 the clearest expression of monotheism in the Hebrew Bible. A scribe in the Gospels repeats the words to Jesus (Mark 12:32).

a: create disaster
p: The KJV has 'I make peace, and create evil'. The word here is the opposite of 'peace', so most versions say 'disaster'.
b: Ra' covers both moral evil and harm, misfortune, calamity. Here it stands opposite shalom, 'peace, well-being', as darkness stands opposite light, so most translators read 'disaster, trouble' (as in Amos 3:6, "Does disaster fall on a city and the LORD has not done it?", and Lamentations 3:38). The verse claims that nothing, prosperity or ruin, lies outside the LORD's rule; it is the climax of the Cyrus oracle, in which God sends both the conqueror and the fall of Babylon. Ra' is also the ordinary Hebrew word for 'evil' ("call evil good", 5:20), and the Greek (poiōn kaka, 'making evils') and the Latin (creans malum, 'creating evil') both say 'evil', so 'disaster' is a judgment from the context, not something the dictionary forces. The KJV's 'evil' is a fair rendering of the word. Most interpreters hold that the verse speaks of calamity sent by God, not of moral evil, but the verse does not itself say so, and the church's answers differ (see the card on this page). Some scholars hear a rebuttal of a Persian belief in two rival powers of light and darkness; others doubt that this belief was Cyrus's or that the prophet knew it.

a: I make peace
t: "Who makes peace and creates all things"
p: The synagogue's morning blessing quotes this verse but changes 'evil' to 'all things'.
b: The first blessing before the Shema in the morning service, Yotser Or, begins: "Blessed are you, LORD our God, King of the universe, who forms light and creates darkness, who makes peace and creates all things." The Talmud explains the change: the verse says 'evil', but the blessing says 'all things' as a more fitting expression (Babylonian Talmud, Berakhot 11b). Israel praised God as maker of light and darkness every morning, while avoiding saying aloud that he creates evil.

a: clouds, let righteousness stream down
p: In Isaiah 40–55 'righteousness' often means God's saving action: it pairs with 'salvation'.
b: Tsedeq and tsedaqah usually mean what is right and just. In Isaiah 40–55 they often mean God's right acts on behalf of his people, his victory and their vindication, and so they stand beside 'salvation' (45:8; 46:13; 51:5–6, 8). The Plain English Translation keeps 'righteousness' here so readers can follow the word, and uses 'saving acts' (45:24) and 'vindication' (54:17) where the context requires. The image is of rain and harvest: rescue comes down from heaven and springs up from the ground. The Latin Vulgate made the rain a person: 'Drop down dew, heavens, from above, and let the clouds rain the righteous one; let the earth open and bud forth a savior.' Sung as Rorate caeli, it became a chant of Advent.

a: Does the clay say to the one who shapes it
p: Paul uses this image in Romans 9; Jeremiah 18 builds a whole sermon on it.
b: The woe answers people who objected to God's plan, probably the plan to save Israel through a pagan king. A pot cannot tell the potter how to work, and a child does not lecture a parent about being born (45:10). Isaiah used the same picture earlier (29:16) and will again in prayer (64:8). Jeremiah watches a potter remake a spoiled pot (Jeremiah 18:1–6). Paul quotes the question in his discussion of God's choice of Israel and the nations (Romans 9:20–21); Wisdom of Solomon 15:7 also uses it.

a: a piece of pottery among the pieces of pottery on the ground
p: The Hebrew is terse and the old translations differ.
b: Literally 'a potsherd with potsherds of the ground'. The Plain English Translation takes it as a description of the one who argues: a mere clay pot, one among many. The KJV supplies verbs ('Let the potsherd strive with the potsherds'), and the Greek makes a different sentence ('Will the plowman plow the ground all day?'), reading choresh 'plowman' for cheres 'pottery'. 1QIsa-a spells the word chwrshy, the spelling of 'plowmen', which shows how early the line was read in two ways.

a: Will you question me about what is coming to my children?
p: The Hebrew reads as two commands, 'Ask me... command me'; most read them as indignant questions.
b: Literally: 'The coming things ask me; about my sons and about the work of my hands command me.' Read as commands, the line is bitter irony: 'Go ahead, give me orders about my children!' Many scholars repoint the first word to make it a question, as the Plain English Translation does, or emend it to 'Will you question me about my children?'. The sense is the same either way: Israel has no standing to dictate how God will save them.

a: set my exiles free
p: Ezra 1 records Cyrus's decree; the cylinder speaks of returning peoples to their homes.
b: Ezra 1:1–4 and 6:3–5 give Cyrus's order allowing Judeans to return and rebuild the temple, with the temple vessels returned (Ezra 1:7–11). The Cyrus Cylinder says Cyrus "collected together all of their people and returned them to their settlements", though it names only cities in Mesopotamia. Isaiah adds that Cyrus will do it "not for a price and not for a payoff": unlike the ransom of 43:3, the LORD needs to pay no one. Cyrus 'will build my city' in the sense that he allowed it to be rebuilt; the walls were built under Nehemiah nearly a century later.

a: Cush
p: Cush is the Nile kingdom south of Egypt, in today's Sudan; the KJV says 'Ethiopia'.
b: Cush was the kingdom of Nubia on the upper Nile, whose kings had ruled Egypt as its 25th Dynasty (about 744–656 BC). The Greek and the KJV call it 'Ethiopia', which in ancient usage meant the Nile lands south of Egypt, not modern Ethiopia. The Sabeans (Seba) were a people of the same region or of Arabia. Herodotus says the Ethiopians were "the tallest and most handsome of all men" (Histories 3.20), which fits "men of great height". The three nations of 43:3, once named as Israel's ransom, now come to Zion themselves. The 'you' is feminine: Zion is addressed.

a: Surely God is among you
p: Paul echoes this confession of the nations when outsiders come into the church's worship.
b: The nations who once oppressed Israel come and confess that the true God is with Zion. Zechariah 8:23 pictures foreigners taking hold of a Jew's robe because "God is with you". Paul uses the words when an outsider hears prophecy in the church and falls down to worship, saying 'God is really among you' (1 Corinthians 14:25).

a: You are indeed a God who keeps himself hidden
p: Who speaks, and what the hiddenness means, are debated; the line became a classic of theology.
b: The speaker may be the nations of 45:14, amazed that Israel's God was at work unseen; or the prophet, or Israel, confessing that God works in ways no one would expect, through a pagan king. Jewish readers have linked it with God's 'hiding his face' in exile (Deuteronomy 31:17–18; 8:17) and with the book of Esther, where God is never named. Luther built on it his teaching of the Deus absconditus, the God who hides himself even in revealing himself, above all in the cross (The Bondage of the Will). Pascal wrote that "a religion which does not affirm that God is hidden is not true" (Pensées). The Greek reads differently: "For you are God, and we did not know it."

a: He did not create it to be shapeless
p: The word tohu here is the 'shapeless' of Genesis 1:2. The 'gap theory' built on this verse.
b: Tohu is the word in Genesis 1:2, "The earth was shapeless and empty." Isaiah says God did not create the earth to stay tohu; he formed it to be lived in. The point is purpose: God's creation aims at life, so the exiles' land will not stay empty either (compare 49:19; 54:3). In the 1800s and 1900s some readers (Thomas Chalmers, and the Scofield Reference Bible) took the verse to prove that God first made a perfect earth that later became tohu, perhaps through Satan's fall, so that a long gap separates Genesis 1:1 and 1:2. Most interpreters, conservative and critical, read the verse as a statement of God's goal, not a hidden history of two creations.

a: Look for me in the void
p: God's word was spoken openly, unlike the secret arts of diviners and the oracles of the dead.
b: The same word tohu returns: God did not send Israel to search for him 'in emptiness', in vain. Diviners consulted spirits in dark places and spoke in whispers (8:19; 29:4). The LORD's word was public, and its fulfillment can be checked (45:21). On this site 'the void' keeps the link with 45:18.

a: you survivors of the nations
p: Probably those of the nations who live through Cyrus's conquests, now invited to turn to the LORD.
b: Pelite haggoyim, 'escapees of the nations', is unusual. Most read it of those who survive the fall of empires, called to a trial where their idols will be shown helpless (45:20–21) and then invited to be saved (45:22). Some think it means Israelites scattered among the nations. The first reading suits 45:22–23, where 'all the ends of the earth' are called.

a: Turn to me, all you ends of the earth, and be saved
t: An invitation to the whole world
p: The LORD's salvation is offered beyond Israel. The verse also changed the life of a famous preacher.
b: Having shown that the idols cannot save, the LORD invites every nation to turn. The Hebrew verb penu means to turn the face toward someone; the KJV renders it 'Look unto me'. On a snowy Sunday in January 1850 the teenage Charles Spurgeon heard a lay preacher at a small Primitive Methodist chapel in Colchester, England, preach on this verse in the KJV's wording, and he dated his conversion to that morning.

a: every knee will bend before me
p: Paul applies this oath of the LORD to God's judgment (Romans 14) and to Jesus (Philippians 2).
b: In Romans 14:11 Paul quotes the verse in the Greek's wording, 'every tongue will confess to God', to say that all will stand before God's judgment. In Philippians 2:10–11 he says that at the name of Jesus "every knee will bow" and "every tongue confess that Jesus Christ is Lord". There he takes words that the LORD swears about himself alone ("apart from me there is no God", 45:21) and applies them to Jesus. Scholars such as Richard Bauckham see this as one of the clearest places where the earliest Christians included Jesus in the identity of Israel's one God. Jewish readers take the verse as the nations' future acknowledgment of the LORD (Zephaniah 3:9; Zechariah 14:9), and its words are said every day in the Aleinu prayer.

a: will be in the right
t: In the right through the LORD
p: The verb is the root Paul renders 'justify'.
b: Yitsdequ, 'they will be in the right, be vindicated', is the court word for winning one's case; it is the plain (Qal) form, 'be in the right', not the Hiphil 'put in the right' of 50:8. The Greek has dikaiōthēsontai, 'they will be justified', the verb of Paul's teaching that people are put right with God by faith (Romans 3:24–26). In Isaiah the vindication comes "through the LORD": Israel's standing comes from God's saving act, not its own strength (45:24).

a: Bel has bowed down; Nebo is doubled over
p: Bel is Marduk, the god of Babylon; Nebo is Nabu, his son, the god of writing at nearby Borsippa.
b: Bel, 'lord', was the title of Marduk, Babylon's chief god; Nabu (Nebo), god of scribes, was his son. Their names are part of the kings' names Nebuchadnezzar (Nabu-kudurri-usur) and Nabonidus (Nabu-na'id). At the New Year festival their statues were carried in a great procession through Babylon. Isaiah turns the procession into a flight: the images are loaded on tired animals and hauled off as captives. The Nabonidus Chronicle reports that before Cyrus arrived the gods of other cities were brought into Babylon, and the Cyrus Cylinder says Cyrus sent them home. Babylon's own gods were not carried off by Cyrus, who honored Marduk; the picture is a taunt of their helplessness, not a report of 539 BC.

a: you whom I have carried since you were in the belly
t: Gods who are carried, and the God who carries
p: Babylon carries its gods; the LORD has carried Israel from birth and will carry them into old age.
b: The chapter turns on one verb. The idols are a load (46:1–2), hoisted on shoulders (46:7); the LORD is the one who carries (46:3–4). He has borne Israel since the womb and will still carry them when their hair is gray. Deuteronomy uses the same picture: "the LORD your God carried you, the way a man carries his son" (Deuteronomy 1:31); compare the eagle's wings of Exodus 19:4 and 63:9. The image of God as a mother carrying a child returns at 49:15 and 66:13.

a: I am he
p: The short Hebrew phrase ani hu is the LORD's self-naming in these chapters; the Greek renders it 'I am'.
b: Ani hu, literally 'I [am] he', means 'I am the one', the same one through all of history (41:4; 43:10, 13, 25; 48:12; 52:6). The Greek translates it egō eimi, 'I am'. In the Gospel of John, Jesus uses the same Greek words absolutely ("unless you believe that I am", John 8:24, 28, 58; 13:19), and many scholars hear Isaiah's phrase behind them, alongside Exodus 3:14. Jewish liturgy uses ani hu as a divine name in the Hoshana prayers of Sukkot (Mishnah Sukkah 4:5, ani vaho).

a: weigh silver on a balance
p: An idol was paid for by weight of metal and made to order by a craftsman.
b: Before coins, silver was weighed out on a balance (Genesis 23:16; Jeremiah 32:9–10). The worshipers buy the metal, hire a goldsmith, and then bow down to the thing they paid for. Isaiah has made the same argument at length (40:18–20; 44:9–20). In Babylon itself a new or repaired statue went through the 'mouth-washing' and 'mouth-opening' rites, which were believed to make the god present in it; the prophet sees only metal and wages.

a: hold steady
p: The Hebrew verb is unique and its meaning is guessed from context.
b: Hit'oshashu occurs nowhere else. The KJV, linking it with 'ish, 'man', has 'shew yourselves men'; others connect it with a root 'be firm' or 'found', as the Plain English Translation does. The Greek has 'groan', the Latin 'be ashamed'. The point is plain enough: the rebels are to think again and stand firm in what they know.

a: From the beginning I announce the end
p: Only the true God can say in advance what he will do; on this the whole argument with the idols rests.
b: Chapters 41–48 return to this test again and again: the idols cannot announce "the first things" or what is coming (41:21–29; 43:9; 44:7; 45:21; 48:3–6). Readers holding the traditional view see the naming of Cyrus as the sharpest example, given more than a century ahead. Readers holding the critical view hear the prophet pointing to earlier prophecies now fulfilled and to Cyrus's rise as proof that the LORD directs history. On either view the claim is the same: the LORD's plan stands, and what he wants, he does.

a: I call a bird of prey from the east
t: A bird of prey from the east
p: Cyrus is the swooping hunter; Xenophon says a golden eagle was the Persian king's standard.
b: Cyrus came from Persia, east of Babylon (41:2, 25). The 'ayit is a bird that swoops on carcasses (Genesis 15:11), an image of speed and of a hunter no one can resist. Xenophon, writing about 370 BC, says the royal standard of Cyrus was a golden eagle with wings spread, mounted on a long shaft (Cyropaedia 7.1.4). The second line names the bird plainly: 'the man of my plan'. The Hebrew has 'my plan' as read aloud (Qere) and 'his plan' as written (Ketiv); see the variant.

a: I am bringing my righteousness near
p: God's 'righteousness' and 'salvation' are one thing here: his rescue, now at hand.
b: As at 45:8, 'righteousness' is God's right action on his people's behalf, and 'salvation' is its result. To the stubborn who think rescue is far off (46:12), the LORD answers that it is near and will not be delayed. Paul uses the language of nearness for the gospel (Romans 10:8; 13:11–12), and 51:5 and 56:1 repeat the promise.

a: virgin Daughter Babylon
p: A city is pictured as a young woman; 'virgin' means a city never yet taken.
b: Hebrew poetry speaks of a city or nation as a daughter: Daughter Zion, Daughter Sidon (23:12), Daughter Egypt (Jeremiah 46:11). 'Virgin' adds that she had never been captured: Babylon had ruled for nearly seventy years since Nebuchadnezzar's victories. The phrase is used here with heavy irony. The chapter is a reversal of Zion's: Babylon goes down from a throne into the dust (47:1), while Zion rises from the dust to sit enthroned (52:2).

a: Take a hand mill and grind meal
p: Grinding grain was the work of the lowest slave women; crossing the rivers is the march into exile.
b: In the ancient Near East grain was ground daily on a hand mill of two stones, the task of slave girls and captives (Exodus 11:5; Judges 16:21; Matthew 24:41). Lady Babylon must take off her veil, the mark of a free woman, tuck up her skirt and wade the rivers on foot as a deportee. The humiliation of 47:3 continues the image: a conquered city was likened to a woman stripped and shamed (Nahum 3:5).

a: and no human being will stand in my way
p: The Hebrew is clipped and can be read several ways.
b: Lo' 'efga' 'adam means literally 'I will not meet a man'. The verb paga' means to meet, encounter, or intercede. The Plain English Translation takes it as 'no one will intercept me'; others read 'I will spare no one' (the Latin), 'I will not let anyone plead with me', or, with the Greek, 'I will no longer hand you over to men'. The KJV's "I will not meet thee as a man" makes God's meeting unlike any human encounter. All agree the line announces judgment without appeal.

a: Our redeemer
p: The worshipers interrupt the taunt to praise the God who acts for them.
b: The verse is a chorus inside the LORD's speech: "our redeemer" is Israel's response. A go'el was the close relative who bought back a family member or land and avenged a death (Leviticus 25:25; Numbers 35:19; Ruth 4:4–6). Isaiah 40–55 gives the title to God thirteen times (41:14; 43:14; 44:6). Here the redeemer's act is to bring down the power that holds his people.

a: I treated my own inheritance as common
t: Punished, but not to be crushed
p: God gave his people into Babylon's hand, but Babylon went beyond its commission.
b: The LORD admits that he handed Judah over in anger (42:24–25), and that the exile was his judgment. Babylon's guilt is that it showed no pity, even to the old. The same pattern appears with Assyria, the rod in God's hand that boasts against him (10:5–15), and in Zechariah 1:15: "I was only a little angry, but they helped make the harm worse." Lamentations 5:12 remembers that "the faces of elders were not respected".

a: I am, and besides me there is nothing
p: Babylon's boast takes the LORD's own words; Revelation gives the same boast to the city it names Babylon.
b: Babylon says ani ve'afsi 'od, 'I, and there is no other besides me', echoing what the LORD alone says of himself (45:5–6, 18, 21–22; 46:9). Zephaniah 2:15 puts the same words in the mouth of Nineveh. Babylon also boasts that she will never be a widow or lose her children, and in one day she loses both (47:9). Revelation 18:7–8 takes up the scene for the city it calls Babylon: "In her heart she says, 'I sit as a queen. I am not a widow, and I will never see grief.'" Her plagues also come "in one day".

a: for all your many sorceries
p: Babylon was famous for incantation, divination and star-lore; the prophet calls them useless.
b: Babylonian religion had a large professional class of exorcists (ashipu) and diviners (baru), with written collections of incantations (the series Maqlu, 'Burning', and Shurpu) and thousands of omens read from livers, births and the sky. Isaiah lists them in turn: sorceries and spells (47:9, 12), the charms that might avert disaster (47:11), the star-watchers (47:13). Daniel's court of "magicians, enchanters, sorcerers and Chaldeans" belongs to the same world (Daniel 2:2).

a: and you will not know how to charm it away
t: Charm it away, or its dawn?
p: The Hebrew shachrah is read as 'its dawn' (KJV) or as a word for charming away.
b: The KJV reads shachrah as 'its dawn' ("thou shalt not know from whence it riseth"). Many modern scholars hear a second word shachar, 'to charm or bribe' (compare Akkadian and the parallel kapperah, 'to buy it off, appease it'), so that both lines say Babylon's magic cannot turn the disaster aside. The Plain English Translation follows that reading. The Hebrew allows both; the line plays on Babylon's skill in averting evil omens.

a: the ones who map out the sky
p: Babylon's astronomers kept records of the sky for centuries and read them as omens for the king.
b: Hoverei shamayim probably means 'dividers of the sky', those who marked the heavens into sections and constellations (the written Hebrew has hovru, the read form hovrei). The Babylonian 'astronomical diaries' recorded the night sky almost every night for centuries; the oldest surviving diary dates from 652 BC, and the series may reach back to about 750 BC, and the great omen series Enuma Anu Enlil told what each sign meant for king and country. Monthly reports went to the Assyrian kings. Isaiah mocks the system: the stars could not tell Babylon what was about to fall on it. By Hellenistic times 'Chaldean' meant an astrologer (Daniel 2:2, 10).

a: who traded with you since your youth
p: Babylon's trading partners abandon her; Revelation's merchants stand far off and mourn.
b: The 'traders' (socharayikh) are the merchants who grew rich through Babylon. When she falls, each goes off his own way. Revelation 18:11–19 develops the picture for the later 'Babylon', where "the merchants of the earth weep and mourn over her, because no one buys their cargo anymore" (Revelation 18:11). Ezekiel 27 gives a similar lament over Tyre.

a: who came from the waters of Judah
p: The phrase means descent from Judah; some read 'from the loins of Judah' with a small change.
b: Hebrew can speak of descent as flowing from a spring ("from Israel's fountain", Psalm 68:26; "Jacob's spring", Deuteronomy 33:28). Many scholars instead read mimme'e, 'from the body (loins) of', a change of one letter (compare 48:19). The Greek has simply 'who come out of Judah'. Either way, the line names Israel's pedigree, which the end of the verse turns against them: they swear by the LORD, but not in truth.

a: The first things I announced long ago
t: The first things and the new things
p: Isaiah sets 'the first things', already foretold and fulfilled, against the 'new things' now announced.
b: The pair runs through 40–48 (41:22; 42:9; 43:9, 18–19; 46:9; 48:3, 6). Traditional readers take 'the first things' as earlier prophecies fulfilled in Israel's history, and the 'new things' as Cyrus and the return, announced long before. Critical readers often take 'the first things' as Cyrus's early victories, already happening, and the 'new things' as the fall of Babylon and the release. In both, the purpose is pastoral: Israel is stubborn (48:4, 8), so God told them ahead of time, to leave no room to thank an idol (48:5).

a: your neck is a cord of iron
p: A stiff neck will not bow; a brow of bronze will not blush.
b: A 'stiff-necked' people is one that will not bend under the yoke or turn its head when called (Exodus 32:9; Deuteronomy 31:27). The brow is the place of shame: Jeremiah speaks of a prostitute's brow that will not blush (Jeremiah 3:3). Ezekiel is given a forehead harder than flint to match his hearers (Ezekiel 3:7–9). The LORD's frankness here explains why he spoke so far in advance (48:5).

a: the furnace of misery
p: Egypt was the 'iron furnace'; Babylon is another furnace in which God refines his people.
b: Deuteronomy calls Egypt "the iron furnace" from which the LORD took Israel to be his people (Deuteronomy 4:20; 1 Kings 8:51; Jeremiah 11:4). Exile is the same: suffering that refines rather than destroys. 'Not as silver' probably means the refining was not carried as far as a silversmith would carry it, for then nothing would be left (compare 1:22, 25; Jeremiah 6:29–30). Where the Hebrew has 'chosen' in the second line, the Great Isaiah Scroll has 'tested'; see the variant.
r: 1:25; Deuteronomy 4:20; 1 Kings 8:51; Jeremiah 11:4; Jeremiah 6:29–30; Zechariah 13:9; Malachi 3:3; 1 Peter 1:7

a: I do not hand my glory to anyone else
p: God acts for his own name's sake, so that no idol can claim the credit.
b: The line repeats 42:8. The LORD saves Israel not because they deserve it (48:8) but for the sake of his name (48:9, 11), a theme Ezekiel develops at length (Ezekiel 20:9, 14, 22; 36:22). The idea is not vanity but truth-telling: if Israel were saved and an idol thanked, the world would be told a lie about who rules history.

a: I am first; I am last as well
p: The title returns from 41:4 and 44:6; Revelation gives it to the risen Jesus.
b: The LORD is 'first' and 'last' because he was there before history and will be there after it (41:4; 44:6). The Greek makes the second half 'I am forever'. In Revelation the risen Jesus says: "I am the First and the Last" (Revelation 1:17; 2:8), and at the end, "I am the Alpha and the Omega, the First and the Last, the Beginning and the End" (Revelation 22:13).

a: The LORD loves him
p: The man God loves is Cyrus; the Greek turns the line into God's love for Israel.
b: The Hebrew YHWH 'ahevo says that the LORD loves Cyrus, who will do his will against Babylon. Some read 'the one the LORD loves' as a title, as for Solomon (2 Samuel 12:24–25). 1QIsa-a reads 'those who love me'. The Greek has 'Because I love you, I have done your will', addressed to Israel. The Hebrew line is bold: the foreign king who does not know the LORD (45:4) is loved for the task he is given.

a: And now the Lord GOD has sent me, and his Spirit
t: Who is speaking, and who is sent?
p: A new voice speaks at the end of the verse, and the grammar lets 'his Spirit' be either a sender or one who is sent.
b: Up to this point the LORD speaks; suddenly 'I' is someone the Lord GOD has sent. Many think the prophet speaks; others hear the servant, who speaks again in 49:1. The Hebrew can mean 'the Lord GOD has sent me, together with his Spirit' (the Spirit also sends) or 'has sent me and his Spirit' (both are sent). The Targum has 'the LORD God and his Memra have sent me'. Origen quotes the verse to show the Spirit sending the prophets (Against Celsus 1.46), and many church writers read it as a glimpse of Father, Son and Spirit. Most modern scholars read it as the prophet's claim to his commission, as at 61:1.

a: Your peace would have flowed like a river
p: A rare lament on God's lips: what Israel would have had, if they had listened.
b: The Hebrew lu', 'if only', looks back with regret. The sentence echoes Deuteronomy's choice of life or death (Deuteronomy 5:29; 32:29) and Psalm 81:13–16. The images of a river and the waves of the sea return in 66:12, where peace flows to Jerusalem like a river after all. 'Righteousness' here is the right order of life in a people who keep God's commands. The promise of children as many as the sand (48:19) recalls Abraham (Genesis 22:17).

a: Go out from Babylon
p: The call to leave Babylon is the climax of 40–48; Jeremiah and Revelation repeat it.
b: The command closes the Cyrus chapters: the exiles are to walk out of Babylon, as their ancestors walked out of Egypt, and tell the world. Jeremiah gives the same call (Jeremiah 50:8; 51:6, 45), and Isaiah repeats it at 52:11–12. Revelation sounds it again for its own Babylon: "Come out of her, my people, ... so that you have no part in her sins ... and receive none of her plagues" (Revelation 18:4). Not all the exiles came; many stayed in Babylonia, where a great Jewish community lived for the next 2,500 years.
r: 52:11–12; Jeremiah 50:8; Jeremiah 51:6; Jeremiah 51:45; Zechariah 2:6–7; Revelation 18:4; Ezra 1:5

a: He made water trickle from a rock for them
p: The new journey home is told in the words of the old journey out of Egypt.
b: In the wilderness Moses struck the rock at Horeb and water came out (Exodus 17:6; Numbers 20:11; Psalm 78:15–16; Psalm 105:41). Isaiah applies the old story to the return across the desert from Babylon, as he did at 41:18 and 43:19–20. Paul reads the rock as a figure of Christ (1 Corinthians 10:4). The picture is of an exodus repeated, so that the exiles would hear their own release as a second deliverance from Egypt.

a: The wicked have no peace
t: A refrain that divides the book
p: The same line closes chapter 57, and many readers find three sections of nine chapters in 40–66.
b: The saying comes again, in slightly different words, at 57:21, and 66:24 closes the book with a picture of the wicked. Many commentators, from Franz Delitzsch on, have seen 40–66 as three groups of nine chapters (40–48, 49–57, 58–66), each ending on the fate of the wicked. Here the line warns that release from Babylon is no blessing for those who refuse the LORD who gives it.

a: The LORD called me from the womb
p: The servant's call echoes Jeremiah's; Paul describes his own call in the same words.
b: The second servant song (49:1–6, often taken to 49:13) is spoken by the servant himself, to the far coasts and peoples. Like Jeremiah ("before I formed you in the belly I knew you", Jeremiah 1:5), he was named and chosen before birth. Paul tells the Galatians that God "set me apart from my mother's womb and called me by his grace" to proclaim his Son among the nations (Galatians 1:15–16), borrowing the servant's words and his mission to the nations (49:6) for his own. Luke gives Jesus a name announced before his birth (Luke 1:31; 2:21).

a: He made my mouth a sharp sword
p: The servant's weapon is his word; Revelation shows a sword coming from the mouth of Christ.
b: The servant conquers by speaking, like the shoot of Jesse who whose "mouth will be a rod to strike the earth" (11:4). He is a polished arrow kept hidden in the quiver until the moment for it comes. Revelation pictures the risen Jesus with "a sharp two-edged sword" coming out of his mouth (Revelation 1:16; 19:15), and Hebrews 4:12 and Ephesians 6:17 call God's word a sword.

a: Israel; through you I will win glory
p: The servant is named 'Israel', yet in 49:5–6 he is sent to bring Israel back. Who is he?
b: Elsewhere in 40–48 the servant is plainly the people Israel (41:8; 44:1, 21; 45:4). Here the name stands again, yet the servant has a mission to Jacob (49:5–6). Readings: (1) The people Israel, or the faithful part of it, called to restore the rest and to be a light to the nations. This is the main Jewish reading (Rashi, Ibn Ezra, Kimchi). (2) An individual who embodies Israel, the one in whom Israel's calling is fulfilled; many Christian readers see Christ as this true Israel, as Matthew applies Israel's story to Jesus (Matthew 2:15). (3) The prophet himself, given Israel's name and task (some modern scholars; compare 49:4). (4) 'Israel' as a later addition: one medieval Hebrew manuscript, Kennicott 96, lacks the word, but every scroll from Qumran and the Greek have it, so few now delete it. See the deep section on chapter 49.

a: I have worked hard for nothing
p: The servant's complaint of wasted effort is answered by a wider mission; Paul uses the same language.
b: The servant's first words are discouragement: leriq yaga'ti, 'for emptiness I have labored'. His comfort is that his case and his reward lie with God, not with visible success. The answer that follows is not rest but a larger task (49:6). Paul uses the language of laboring 'in vain' of his own work among the churches (Galatians 2:2; Philippians 2:16; 1 Corinthians 15:58), and the mood recalls Elijah's despair (1 Kings 19:4) and Jeremiah's complaints (Jeremiah 20:7–9).

a: I will give you as a light to the nations
p: Restoring Israel is too small a task; the servant's light is for the whole world. Simeon and Paul quote it.
b: Naqel, 'it is too light a thing', sets two tasks side by side: to restore the tribes of Jacob, and to bring God's salvation to the ends of the earth. The second takes up 42:6. In Luke, the old man Simeon, holding the infant Jesus, calls him "a light to bring revelation to the nations, / and glory to Israel your people" (Luke 2:32). In Acts, Paul and Barnabas turn to the Gentiles at Pisidian Antioch and quote this verse as the Lord's command to them: 'I have made you a light for the nations, so that you will bring salvation to the end of the earth' (Acts 13:47, close to the Greek). Acts 1:8 and 26:23 echo it as well. Jewish readers hear Israel's vocation among the nations (compare 42:6; 60:3).

a: to one whom people despise
p: The servant despised by the nations will see kings rise; 52:13–53:12 tells the same story at length.
b: The servant is bezoh nefesh, 'despised of soul', loathed by the nation, a slave of rulers. 'Slave' is 'eved, the same word as 'servant' in 49:3, 5 and 6 and throughout 40–55: the line is the song's own reminder that the servant of the LORD is, in the eyes of the powerful, a slave. The words look ahead to 53:3 ("he was despised", the same root) and to 52:15, where kings shut their mouths before him. The reversal is God's doing: he 'keeps faith' and 'has chosen you'. Those who read the servant as Israel hear exiled Israel, despised among the nations; others hear an individual.

a: When the time of favor came, I answered you
p: Paul quotes this line and says the time it speaks of has come.
b: In 2 Corinthians 6:2 Paul quotes the line word for word from the Greek ('At a time of favor I listened to you, and on a day of salvation I helped you') and adds: 'Look, now is the time of favor; look, now is the day of salvation.' He uses it to urge the Corinthians not to receive God's grace in vain. The 'time of favor' ('et ratson) is close to "a year of the LORD's goodwill" in 61:2, which Jesus reads in Nazareth (Luke 4:19).

a: and make you a covenant of the people
p: The phrase from 42:6 returns; the servant does not just bring the covenant but is it.
b: Berit 'am is unusual Hebrew. It may mean that the servant embodies God's covenant with his people, or that he is the mediator through whom the covenant is renewed; some take 'am as 'humanity' (compare 42:5), making the servant a covenant for all people. Here the task is to resettle the ruined land and give out its plots again, as Joshua did (Joshua 13–19). The Greek has "a covenant of nations".

a: to tell the prisoners, "Out you come,"
p: The servant's work frees captives, as in 42:7 and 61:1.
b: The exiles are prisoners in the dark; the return is a release from jail (42:7; 61:1). Jesus reads 61:1–2 in the synagogue at Nazareth and says it is fulfilled in his hearing (Luke 4:18–21). The release is followed by the picture of a flock grazing safely along the way home, with the LORD as shepherd (40:11).

a: They will not go hungry or thirsty
p: Revelation gives these words to the crowd from every nation before God's throne.
b: Isaiah describes the journey home: no hunger, no thirst, no sharav (the scorching heat, or the shimmering mirage of 35:7) and no sun to strike them. Revelation 7:16–17 takes the promise up for the great crowd from every nation: "They will never be hungry again or thirsty again. The sun will not beat down on them, nor any burning heat. The Lamb in the center of the throne will be their shepherd. He will lead them to springs of the water of life." Psalm 121:6 and Psalm 23 share the images.

a: Zion said, "The LORD has left me;
p: Zion's lament opens the second of the seven synagogue readings of consolation.
b: From here the speeches turn from the servant to Zion, the city pictured as a mother who has lost her children. Her words answer Lamentations, which ends: 'Why do you keep forgetting us, leaving us for days without end?' (Lamentations 5:20). In the synagogue, 49:14–51:3 is the haftarah for the Sabbath of Ekev, the second of the seven readings of consolation read in the weeks after the Ninth of Av, the fast for the Temple's destruction. The Midrash Pesikta de-Rav Kahana builds a sermon on Zion's complaint.

a: Can a woman forget her nursing baby
p: God's love is compared to a nursing mother's, then said to go beyond it.
b: The image is one of the Bible's boldest for God: a woman cannot forget the child she nurses, and even if she could, the LORD will not forget Zion. The word for 'pity' (rachem) is formed from rechem, 'womb'. Isaiah uses the same image again in 66:13 ("Like someone whose mother comforts him, so I myself will comfort you"), and 42:14 pictures God crying out like a woman in labor. Jesus speaks of longing to gather Jerusalem's children like a hen gathering her chicks (Matthew 23:37).

a: Look, I have carved you on the palms of my hands
p: The verb is used for carving inscriptions; the image may be drawn from marks cut or written on the hand.
b: Chaqqotikh, 'I have engraved you', is the verb for carving letters in stone or metal (22:16; Ezekiel 4:1). People sometimes wrote a name or sign on the hand to show whose they were (44:5), and Israel was told to bind God's words on the hand as a reminder (Deuteronomy 6:8). Here the reverse: God marks Zion on his own palms, so that her walls are always before his eyes. Christian devotion has linked the verse with the wounds in Jesus's hands (John 20:27), a reading of later faith, not the prophet's own picture.
r: 44:5; 22:16; Deuteronomy 6:8; Song of Songs 8:6; Exodus 28:9–12; John 20:27

a: fasten them on as a bride does
p: Zion's returning children are her jewels; the bride image returns in 61:10 and 62:5.
b: The returning exiles are like ornaments that a bride ties on for her wedding. The LORD swears by his own life ("By my life"), the strongest oath. The bride image is developed in 54:5–6, 61:10 and 62:4–5, and Revelation shows the new Jerusalem "made ready like a bride dressed in her finery for her husband" (Revelation 21:2). The first lines of the verse return word for word in 60:4.

a: I had lost my children and was barren
p: Zion, bereaved and childless, wakes to find herself surrounded by children she did not bear.
b: The city that thought itself barren and widowed (compare 47:8–9, where Babylon suffers exactly this) is amazed at the crowd of children returning to her. The image prepares for 54:1 ("Sing, barren one") and recalls the barren mothers of Israel's story, Sarah above all (51:2), and Hannah (1 Samuel 2:5). Paul quotes 54:1 of the 'Jerusalem above' in Galatians 4:27.

a: Kings will be your guardians
p: The KJV's 'kings shall be thy nursing fathers' became a text for the state's duty to the church.
b: 'Omenim are guardians or foster fathers who carry and raise children (Numbers 11:12; Ruth 4:16), and the queens are wet nurses. The picture is of nations serving Zion's restoration, as Cyrus did (Ezra 1). The KJV's 'nursing fathers' was used for centuries to argue that rulers must protect and support the true church. The Westminster Confession (1646) cited this verse for the magistrate's duty in religion (23.3), and the American Presbyterian revision of 1788, which rejected state control of the church, still spoke of magistrates 'as nursing fathers' protecting all churches equally. To "lick up the dust" is an image of total submission (Psalm 72:9; Micah 7:17).

a: I will feed your oppressors their own flesh
p: The oppressors will turn on each other, so that the world will know who rescued Israel.
b: Eating one's own flesh pictures civil war and collapse from within (9:20; Zechariah 11:9). 'Sweet wine' ('asis) is new, freshly pressed wine. The verse ends with the purpose of it all: 'all flesh will know' the LORD as Israel's savior and redeemer, the "Mighty One of Jacob", the title from Jacob's blessing (Genesis 49:24), which returns in 60:16.

a: Where are the divorce papers
p: Under Deuteronomy's law a husband gave a written certificate; God has given none, so the marriage stands.
b: Deuteronomy 24:1 describes a husband who "writes her a certificate of divorce, puts it in her hand, and sends her away"; after that she could not return to him (Deuteronomy 24:4). Debt could also force a father to sell his children (2 Kings 4:1; Nehemiah 5:5). God asks for the paper and the creditor: neither exists. Mother Zion was sent away for her sins, but not divorced, and God has no debts. Jeremiah 3:8 says the LORD did give the northern kingdom a certificate, yet invites even her back (Jeremiah 3:12–14). Jesus discusses the same law in Matthew 5:31–32 and 19:7–9.
r: 54:6–7; Deuteronomy 24:1–4; Jeremiah 3:1; Jeremiah 3:8; Hosea 2:2; 2 Kings 4:1; Matthew 19:7–9

a: Is my hand too short to ransom you?
p: God asks why no one answered, and points to his power over sea and rivers.
b: The question repeats what the LORD asked Moses in the wilderness: "Is the LORD's hand too short?" (Numbers 11:23), and 59:1 answers it: "the LORD's hand has not grown too short to save". The proof is the exodus: the sea dried up at his rebuke (Exodus 14:21; Psalm 106:9) and the Nile's fish died and stank (Exodus 7:18, 21). Darkness and sackcloth on the sky (50:3) recall the plague of darkness (Exodus 10:21–23) and look ahead to Revelation's sun "black like sackcloth made of hair" (Revelation 6:12).
r: 59:1; Numbers 11:23; Exodus 14:21; Exodus 7:18; Exodus 10:21–23; Psalm 106:9; Revelation 6:12

a: The Lord GOD has given me a learner's tongue
p: The servant speaks well because he listens first: limmudim means 'those who are taught'.
b: Leshon limmudim is literally 'the tongue of the taught', a disciple's tongue; the same word ends the verse ('as learners do') and recurs in 8:16 ('my disciples') and 54:13 ('the LORD's learners'). The next words, la'ut 'et-ya'ef davar, are uncertain: la'ut occurs only here, and 'to hold up the tired with a word' is a guess from context. The Greek reads 'to know when to speak a word'. Each morning God wakes the servant's ear. Jesus's invitation to the weary (Matthew 11:28) is often heard against this verse.

a: and I did not resist
p: Israel is deaf (42:18–20; 48:8); the servant's ear is open and he does not draw back.
b: Where Israel's 'ear has not been open' (48:8), the servant's has been opened. Psalm 40:6, "ears you have dug for me", makes the same contrast between obedience and sacrifice, and Hebrews 10:5–7 applies that psalm to Jesus. The servant's obedience leads straight into suffering (50:6), which is why the third song is often called the servant's Gethsemane.

a: My back I gave to the floggers
p: The Gospels tell of Jesus beaten, slapped and spat on, in words that echo the Greek of this verse.
b: Pulling out a man's beard was a deep insult (2 Samuel 10:4–5; Nehemiah 13:25), and spitting in the face was public shame (Numbers 12:14; Deuteronomy 25:9). The Greek renders the lines 'I gave my back to whips and my cheeks to blows (rhapismata); I did not turn my face from the shame of spitting'. The Gospels use the same words: Jesus foretells that the Son of Man will be spat on and flogged (Mark 10:34), and at his trial "they spat in his face and punched him, and some slapped him" (Matthew 26:67); "Jesus he had whipped" (Matthew 27:26); compare John 18:22 and 19:1–3. Christians have read the verse as a prophecy of the Passion since the earliest centuries, and it is read in the Catholic liturgy on Palm Sunday. Jewish interpreters such as Rashi and Ibn Ezra take the speaker as the prophet, persecuted for his message.
r: Matthew 26:67; Matthew 27:26; Matthew 27:30; Mark 10:34; Mark 14:65; John 18:22; John 19:1–3; 2 Samuel 10:4–5; Numbers 12:14; Matthew 5:39

a: That is why I have made my face hard as flint
p: The servant's resolve is like Ezekiel's; Luke's 'he set his face to go to Jerusalem' may echo it.
b: Ezekiel's forehead was made "like hard stone, harder than flint" to face a hard-hearted people (Ezekiel 3:8–9). Here the servant sets his face because God is his help, and he knows he will not be put to shame. Luke says that Jesus "set his face" to go to Jerusalem (Luke 9:51), a Hebrew idiom for firm purpose; many commentators hear this verse in it, though the wording is not identical.

a: Near at hand is the one who puts me in the right
p: The servant's courtroom confidence is the pattern for Paul's in Romans 8.
b: The scene is a lawsuit: the servant challenges any accuser to stand with him before the judge, because the judge himself will put him in the right (matsdiqi, 'my justifier'). Paul's triumphant questions follow the same steps and much of the Greek wording: 'Who will bring a charge against God's chosen ones? It is God who justifies. Who is the one who condemns?' (Romans 8:33–34). The verb returns in 53:11, where the servant 'puts the many in the right'.

a: listens to the voice of his servant
p: Only here is the speaker of the third song called 'his servant', which links him with 42 and 49.
b: Verses 4–9 never use the word 'servant'; 50:10 does, and so ties the speaker to the other songs. Rashi and Ibn Ezra take the speaker to be the prophet himself, mocked and beaten for his message; others read Israel; Christians since the New Testament have read Jesus. Verses 10–11 then divide the hearers: those who fear the LORD and trust him in the dark, and those who light their own fires and will lie down in pain. Jesus says, "The one who follows me will never walk around in the dark" (John 8:12).

a: and arm yourselves with flaming arrows
p: The rare word ziqot is read as sparks, firebrands or burning arrows.
b: Me'azzere ziqot means 'those who gird on ziqot'. The word occurs only here and perhaps in Proverbs 26:18 (as ziqqim, 'firebrands'). The KJV has 'compass yourselves about with sparks'; many modern versions say 'firebrands' or 'burning arrows'. The point is self-reliance: those who make their own light will be burned by it, and 'lie down in pain', perhaps in the grave.

a: look at the rock that you were hewn out of
p: Abraham and Sarah are the rock and quarry from which Israel was cut.
b: The exiles who 'chase after righteousness' are told to look back to their origins: Abraham is the rock, Sarah the quarry (51:2 explains the image). One childless couple became a nation; so the few left after the exile can become many again. Ezekiel 33:24 shows the same argument used by those left in the land: 'Abraham was only one man.' John the Baptist warns that descent alone is not enough: "God can raise up children for Abraham from these very stones" (Matthew 3:9), perhaps with a play on this verse.

a: and at Sarah, who went through labor to bear you
t: Sarah, the mother of the people
p: The only place outside Genesis where the Hebrew Bible names Sarah.
b: Sarah is named nowhere else in the Hebrew Bible after Genesis. Here she is the mother in labor, a picture that prepares for 54:1, where the barren one sings. Abraham was 'one' ('echad) when God called him, a word that also hints at the oneness of the God who called. Paul uses the same story of a childless couple made fruitful to describe faith (Romans 4:19) and reads Sarah as the free mother whose children are promised (Galatians 4:22–31, where he quotes Isaiah 54:1). 1 Peter 3:6 calls believing women her daughters.
r: 54:1; Genesis 11:30; Genesis 21:1–7; Romans 4:19; Galatians 4:22–31; 1 Peter 3:6; Hebrews 11:11

a: He makes her wilderness like Eden
p: The ruined land will become like the garden of Genesis 2.
b: Zion's ruins become 'like Eden, like the garden of the LORD' (compare Genesis 13:10, where the Jordan valley is "like the garden of the LORD"). Ezekiel 36:35 says the same of the restored land, and Joel 2:3 reverses it. The return from exile is pictured as a new creation, ending in praise. Revelation's last chapter brings back the river and the tree of life (Revelation 22:1–2).

a: For teaching will go out from me
p: The line echoes 2:3, where teaching goes out from Zion to the nations.
b: Torah here is God's instruction, the guidance he speaks, as in 2:3 ("For from Zion comes teaching") and 42:4 ("the islands are waiting for his teaching"). The site renders it 'teaching' in Isaiah, because it is spoken instruction parallel to God's word; elsewhere it is often the Law of Moses. God's 'justice' becomes 'a light for the peoples', as the servant is (42:6; 49:6). The nations are included in the salvation offered to Israel (51:5).

a: the heavens will blow away like smoke
p: Creation itself will pass away, but God's salvation will not. Jesus says the same of his words.
b: The sky vanishes like smoke, the earth wears out like an old garment (Psalm 102:25–26, quoted in Hebrews 1:10–12). Against this, God's salvation stands forever. The 'gnats' (ken) may also be read 'in like manner' ('they will die in like manner', KJV); the Greek has 'will die like these', and 1QIsa-b writes the two Hebrew words as one, which suits 'likewise'. The Plain English Translation takes the insect, which keeps the run of images. Jesus says: "Heaven and earth will be gone, but my words will never be gone" (Matthew 24:35). 2 Peter 3:10–13 and Revelation 21:1 picture a new heaven and earth (compare 65:17). The Great Isaiah Scroll lacks part of the verse; see the variant.

a: The moth will chew them like a garment
p: Those who scorn God's people will be eaten away like old clothes.
b: The moth ('ash) and the clothes-grub (sas) eat wool slowly but surely (50:9; Job 13:28; Hosea 5:12). Jesus uses the same image of treasure stored on earth, where moth and rust destroy (Matthew 6:19–20), and James 5:2 of the rich whose clothes are moth-eaten. The insults of mortals (51:7) will not last; God's righteousness and salvation, as in 51:6, last from generation to generation.

a: Are you not the one that hacked Rahab apart
p: The LORD's victory over the sea monster is applied to the exodus and to the return.
b: Rahab (rahav, 'the arrogant one', not Rahab of Jericho) and the dragon (tannin) are names for the sea monster of chaos (Job 26:12; Psalm 89:10, "You crushed Rahab like one cut down in battle"; Psalm 74:13). In Babylon's creation epic Enuma Elish, Marduk splits the sea goddess Tiamat; at Ugarit Baal defeats Yam, 'Sea', and the twisting serpent Litan. Isaiah's hearers in Babylon would know Marduk's story. Here, though, the myth is history: 51:10 identifies the victory with the drying of the Red Sea, and 30:7 uses 'Rahab' as a name for Egypt. The prophet uses old imagery to say that Israel's God, not Marduk, conquers the waters. Revelation 12:9 and 20:2 call Satan 'the great dragon'.
r: 30:7; 27:1; Job 26:12; Psalm 89:10; Psalm 74:13–14; Psalm 87:4; Revelation 12:9; Revelation 20:2

a: the waters of the great deep
p: The 'great deep' of creation and the sea of the exodus are one picture here.
b: Tehom rabbah, 'the great deep', is the primeval ocean of Genesis 1:2 ("Darkness lay on the face of the deep") and of the flood (Genesis 7:11). The same God who held back the deep at creation dried the sea for Israel (Exodus 14:21–22; 15:8) and will make a road for the 'redeemed' to come home (35:8–10; 43:16). The verse binds creation, exodus and the return from exile together.

a: The ransomed of the LORD will return
p: The verse repeats 35:10 almost word for word, joining the two halves of the book.
b: The Hebrew here differs from 35:10 only in small points of spelling and grammar, and the Plain English Translation renders both the same. The repetition links the 'highway' promise of 35 with the exodus hymn of 51:9–10. The Great Isaiah Scroll begins the verse differently, with 'the scattered ones of the LORD' (ufzure) for 'the ransomed of the LORD'; 1QIsa-b agrees with the Hebrew. On the 'ransomed', compare 35:10 and 62:12.

a: of a human being who will be made like grass
p: Why fear a mortal, when people are grass and God is the maker of heaven and earth?
b: The comfort of 40:1 returns with "I, I myself, comfort you". The oppressor is only a man who will die, a 'son of Adam' made like grass, as 40:6–8 says ("All flesh is grass... but our God's word will stand forever"). Psalm 103:15–16 and 1 Peter 1:24 use the same image. Fear of man is a kind of forgetting God (51:13).

a: he will not die and go down to the Pit
t: The one stooped under his load
p: The Hebrew line is difficult: tso'eh may mean a prisoner bent double.
b: Tso'eh seems to mean one stooped or bent, a prisoner crouching in chains (compare 63:1, where the same root means 'striding'). The Plain English Translation reads him as a captive soon to be freed, not to die in the dungeon-pit (shachat), and not to lack bread. The KJV has 'the captive exile hasteneth that he may be loosed'. The general sense, release for those in chains, is clear.

a: so as to plant the heavens and found the earth
p: God puts his words in the mouth of his people or his servant, as he did with the prophets.
b: Who is 'you'? The words recall 49:2 (the servant's mouth and the shadow of God's hand) and 59:21, and also God's promise to Moses about a prophet (Deuteronomy 18:18) and to Jeremiah (Jeremiah 1:9). 'To plant the heavens' is an unusual phrase; many scholars think it means 'to stretch out' (as in 51:13) and read lintot for linto'a. The Greek has 'by which I set up the heaven'. Either way, God's word through Israel belongs with his work of creation.

a: the cup of his fury
p: Jerusalem has drunk the cup of God's anger to the bottom; it will now pass to her tormentors.
b: The 'cup' is a common biblical image of the fate God gives to drink (Psalm 75:8; Jeremiah 25:15–29; Ezekiel 23:31–34). Jerusalem has drained it and reels like a drunk. In 51:22–23 the cup is taken from her and given to her oppressors. Revelation uses the image for those who worship the beast: they "will also drink the wine of God's anger, mixed undiluted in the cup of his wrath" (Revelation 14:10). In Gethsemane Jesus prays that 'this cup' might pass from him (Mark 14:36; Matthew 26:39), and Christians have read his words against this background.
r: 51:22–23; Psalm 75:8; Jeremiah 25:15–29; Ezekiel 23:31–34; Revelation 14:10; Revelation 16:19; Matthew 26:39

a: like an antelope in a net
p: The animal is the te'o, probably a wild antelope or oryx, caught struggling in a hunter's net.
b: Te'o appears only here and in the food lists of Deuteronomy 14:5. The Greek has 'like a half-cooked beet', which shows how unsure the early translators were; the Latin has 'oryx'. Most modern scholars take it as an antelope or wild sheep. Jerusalem's young men lie in the streets like a trapped animal exhausted by struggling.

a: Get down on your face so we can cross over you
t: Walking on the backs of the conquered
p: Victors set their feet on the necks or backs of the defeated.
b: Ancient kings were shown with their feet on the necks of enemies (Joshua 10:24; Psalm 110:1; 1 Kings 5:3). Assyrian and Egyptian reliefs show conquered rulers lying flat before the victor. Jerusalem lay in the dust like a road for her conquerors. Now the cup of reeling passes from her to them.

a: For the uncircumcised and the unclean
p: The holy city will never again be entered by an unclean invader; Revelation says the same of the new Jerusalem.
b: 'Wake up, wake up' repeats the call of 51:9 and 51:17, now to Zion herself: she is to dress as a priestly bride in festal robes. The uncircumcised are the foreign armies that broke into the Temple (Lamentations 1:10). Joel 3:17 says that 'strangers will never again pass through her'. Revelation 21:27 says of the new Jerusalem: "Nothing common will ever enter it". Isaiah 56:3–8 later welcomes foreigners who keep the covenant; what is shut out is defilement and conquest.

a: rise and sit, Jerusalem
p: The command looks odd in English: Jerusalem gets up from the dust to sit on a throne.
b: Kumi shevi, 'rise, sit', reverses 47:1, where Babylon is told to come down and sit in the dust without a throne. Some scholars repoint shevi as shevuyah, 'captive', to match 'captive Daughter Zion' in the next line ('Rise, captive Jerusalem'). The Greek has 'rise up and sit, Jerusalem', supporting the Hebrew. The reversal of the two cities is the point.

a: and not with silver will you be bought back
p: As God was paid nothing when he sold his people, he will pay nothing to buy them back.
b: Israel was sent into exile for its sins, not for a price (50:1), so no one holds a claim to be paid off; Cyrus too frees them "not for a price and not for a payoff" (45:13). 1 Peter 1:18–19 echoes the verse: believers were ransomed 'not with perishable things like silver or gold, but with the precious blood of Christ, like that of a lamb' (fresh wording). The ransom language of 53 and the New Testament grows from verses like this.

a: At first my people went down to Egypt
p: Three oppressions are named: Egypt, Assyria, and the present one.
b: The verse is prose, a short survey of Israel's history: they went down to Egypt as guests and were enslaved (Genesis 46; Exodus 1); Assyria crushed the northern kingdom and ravaged Judah (2 Kings 17; 18:13). 'Now' (52:5) is Babylon. Each time the oppressor had no right to them. Some scholars think 52:3–6 is a later prose addition between two poems; others read it as a deliberate pause.

a: my name is treated with contempt
t: God's name blasphemed among the nations
p: Paul quotes the Greek of this line in Romans 2:24.
b: In the Hebrew the nations' rulers mock God's name because his people are captive and seem abandoned. The Greek adds 'because of you' and 'among the nations': 'Because of you my name is blasphemed among the nations'. Paul quotes that Greek form against a Jew who teaches the law but breaks it (Romans 2:24), turning the line around: the dishonor comes from the people's conduct, as in Ezekiel 36:20–23.

a: here I am
p: The word people say when God calls is here said by God himself.
b: Hinneni, 'here I am', is the answer of Abraham (Genesis 22:1, 11), Moses (Exodus 3:4), Samuel (1 Samuel 3:4) and Isaiah (6:8) when God calls. In Isaiah 40–66 God says it to his people (58:9; 65:1). In the day of release they will know his name and recognize him: 'I am he, the one who speaks'.

a: the feet of the one who brings good news
p: The runner bringing news of victory became the Christian messenger of the gospel.
b: A runner comes over the hills toward Jerusalem with news of peace and salvation. Nahum 1:15 has nearly the same line for the fall of Nineveh. Mevasser, 'one who brings good news', is rendered in the Greek euangelizomenos, from which the New Testament's word for 'gospel' (euangelion) comes; 40:9 and 61:1 use the same verb. Paul quotes this verse in Romans 10:15 to say that preachers must be sent so that people may hear and believe: 'How lovely are the feet of those who bring good news!' His wording is closer to the Hebrew than to the Greek. Among the Dead Sea Scrolls, 11QMelchizedek applies the verse to a coming deliverer and calls the messenger 'the anointed of the Spirit'.

a: who tells Zion, "Your God is King!"
p: The cry is the acclamation of the enthronement psalms; the Targum turns it into 'the kingdom of your God is revealed'.
b: Malakh 'Elohayikh uses the same verb as the psalms' shout "The LORD is King!" (Psalm 93:1; 96:10; 97:1; 99:1). The return to Zion is God's coronation: he comes back as king to his city (52:8). The Targum renders it 'the kingdom of your God is revealed', words close to Jesus's announcement that 'the kingdom of God has come near' (Mark 1:15). Many scholars think this verse, with 40:9 and 61:1, lies behind the Gospels' pairing of 'good news' and 'kingdom'.

a: for they will see it eye to eye
p: The idiom means seeing directly, face to face, not 'agreeing'.
b: 'Ayin be'ayin means 'eye into eye', with one's own eyes, as in Numbers 14:14, where the LORD is seen 'eye to eye'. The English phrase 'see eye to eye', meaning 'agree', comes from the KJV of this verse, but the Hebrew means that the lookouts on the walls see the LORD himself returning to Zion. The returning king of 40:9–10 is now in sight.

a: and every far end of the earth
p: The last lines repeat Psalm 98:3, and Luke echoes the thought.
b: The arm 'stripped bare' is a warrior rolling up his sleeve to fight (compare 51:9). The second half matches Psalm 98:3 word for word in the Hebrew, and the Plain English Translation renders both alike ("Every far end of the earth has seen / how our God saves"). The psalm celebrates the LORD as King; Isaiah announces that the act is about to happen. Simeon's words about 'your salvation, which you have prepared in the sight of all peoples' (Luke 2:30–31) echo it, and Luke 3:6 quotes the similar 40:5.

a: Touch nothing unclean
p: Paul quotes these words to call the Corinthians to holiness.
b: The exiles leave like a procession of priests carrying the Temple vessels that Nebuchadnezzar had taken (2 Kings 25:14–15) and Cyrus returned (Ezra 1:7–11). They must be ritually clean, as the Levites were when they carried the holy things (Numbers 4:15). In 2 Corinthians 6:17 Paul combines this verse with others: 'So come out from among them and be separate, says the Lord, and touch nothing unclean, and I will welcome you.' Revelation 18:4 sounds the same call (see 48:20).

a: But you will not go out in a rush
t: Not in a rush this time
p: Unlike the first exodus, eaten 'in a rush', the second will be calm, with God before and behind.
b: Chippazon, 'haste', is the word used for the first Passover: "Eat it in a rush" (Exodus 12:11; Deuteronomy 16:3). The new exodus will not be a flight. As in the old, the LORD goes ahead (Exodus 13:21) and guards the rear (Exodus 14:19, where the angel of God moves behind the camp). The Great Isaiah Scroll adds a line from 54:5; see the variant.

a: my servant
p: The most debated question in the book: Israel, a prophet, the Messiah or Jesus. The chapter page gives each case.
b: The fourth song begins and ends with God speaking (52:13–15; 53:11–12); between them a 'we' confesses that they misjudged the servant (53:1–10). Four main answers: Israel, the people in exile, despised by the nations who will one day confess their error (Rashi, Ibn Ezra, Kimchi, and Origen's Jewish contemporaries); an individual of the past (the prophet himself, Moses, Jeremiah, Zerubbabel, or a martyr of the exile); the Messiah (the Targum, some rabbinic texts); and Jesus, as the New Testament reads it (Acts 8:32–35; 1 Peter 2:22–25). The text itself never names him beyond 'my servant'. The deep section on chapter 53 sets out each reading at its strongest.

a: will succeed
p: Yaskil means both to act wisely and to succeed; the Targum names the servant 'the Messiah'.
b: Yaskil means to act with insight and so to prosper, as David did (1 Samuel 18:14) and as the coming Branch will (Jeremiah 23:5). The Greek has 'my servant will understand'. The Targum of Isaiah, the ancient Aramaic paraphrase read in synagogues, renders the line 'Behold, my servant the Messiah will prosper', one of the clearest messianic readings of the passage in Jewish tradition. As the deep section shows, the Targum also turns the suffering in the passage away from the Messiah onto Israel and the nations.

a: he will be high and lifted up
p: The same pair of verbs describes God's throne in 6:1 and 57:15; John speaks of Jesus being 'lifted up'.
b: Yarum venissa', 'he will be high and lifted up', are the words of Isaiah's vision, and the Plain English Translation renders them the same in all three places: "He was sitting on a throne, high and lifted up" (6:1), and of "the One who is high and lifted up" (57:15). Isaiah elsewhere uses this pair only of God. Many scholars hold that John's Gospel builds on this verse when it speaks of the Son of Man being 'lifted up' on the cross as his glory (John 3:14; 12:32–34), and when, after quoting 53:1, it says that Isaiah "had seen his glory, and it was about him that he spoke" (John 12:41).

a: Just as many were horrified at you
p: God turns from speaking to someone ('you') to speaking about the servant ('his look').
b: The Hebrew, the Great Isaiah Scroll, 4QIsa-c and the Greek all read 'at you'. The Targum and the Syriac have 'at him', and many modern versions follow them for smoothness. Those who keep 'you' take it as Israel addressed (the nations were appalled at Israel's ruin, so the servant's disfigurement mirrors it) or as a sudden address to the servant. The sentence runs on: 'Just as many were horrified... so he will startle many nations' (52:15). The shock of his disfigurement will turn into the shock of his exaltation.

a: so he will startle many nations
p: Yazzeh usually means 'sprinkle', a priest's act; the Greek and many modern versions read 'startle'.
b: The verb hizzah means everywhere else 'to spatter' or 'sprinkle' blood, oil or water in a rite of cleansing (Leviticus 4:6; 16:14; Numbers 19:18–19). Read that way (KJV, 'so shall he sprinkle many nations'), the servant acts as a priest who cleanses the nations, which fits the guilt offering of 53:10 and Ezekiel 36:25. Against it: the verb is always followed by what is sprinkled and 'on' someone, never by people as its object, and the parallel line has kings shutting their mouths in amazement. The Greek reads 'many nations will marvel at him', and many scholars connect yazzeh with an Arabic verb 'to leap', so 'make leap, startle'. All the Qumran copies have the same Hebrew word. The Plain English Translation follows 'startle' as the better match for the parallel; 'sprinkle' remains a strong reading.
r: Leviticus 4:6; Leviticus 16:14; Numbers 19:18–19; Ezekiel 36:25; 1 Peter 1:2; Hebrews 12:24

a: For they will see what no one had told them
p: Paul quotes this line in the Greek to explain why he preaches where Christ is not yet known.
b: The kings fall silent because they see something unheard-of: the despised servant raised high. In Romans 15:21 Paul quotes the line from the Greek ('Those who were not told about him will see, and those who have not heard will understand') as the reason for his plan to preach in places where Christ has not yet been named, such as Spain. Isaiah's kings become Paul's Gentile hearers.

a: Who has believed what we have heard?
p: The speakers who confess their mistake may be the nations and kings of 52:15, or Israel, or the prophet's circle.
b: Shemu'atenu can mean 'what we heard' or 'our report, what we announced' (KJV 'our report'). Rashi, Ibn Ezra and Kimchi hear the nations' kings of 52:15 speaking: they had despised Israel and now confess that Israel suffered for the nations' sins. Many modern scholars agree that the speakers are the nations or the people who misjudged the servant. Christian readers usually hear Israel, or the prophet and his followers, or the church, confessing faith in a rejected Messiah. The answer shapes the whole reading: if 'we' are the nations, the servant is easily Israel; if 'we' are Israel, the servant is someone within or beyond Israel.

a: And the LORD's arm: to whom has it been shown?
p: John and Paul quote this verse to explain why many did not believe the message about Jesus.
b: The LORD's arm, bared before the nations in 52:10, turns out to be revealed in the despised servant, which is why no one believed. The Greek begins the verse with 'Lord', and the New Testament quotes it in that form. John says that despite Jesus's signs people did not believe, "so that the prophet Isaiah's words would come true... 'Lord, who has believed the report we gave? To whom has the Lord's arm been revealed?'" (John 12:38). Paul quotes the first line in Romans 10:16 about Israel's response to the gospel.

a: like a little shoot
p: The servant grows like a sucker from a stump; the image recalls the shoot of Jesse.
b: Yoneq, literally 'a suckling', is a shoot that springs from a root or stump. The parallel 'root from parched ground' pictures something growing where nothing should, small and unpromising. Isaiah 11:1 and 11:10 use related words for the coming king: "From Jesse's stump a shoot will come out" and "the root of Jesse". Christian readers have linked the two passages since the early church; Jewish readers who take the servant as Israel see the nation growing again from the ruins of exile. 'Before him' means before the LORD.

a: He had no stately form or grandeur for us to look at
p: Early Christians debated whether Jesus was plain or even ugly, using this verse; Celsus mocked him for it.
b: The servant had nothing in his appearance to attract anyone, unlike Saul, a head taller than everyone (1 Samuel 9:2), or David, handsome to look at (1 Samuel 16:12), though God "sees the heart" (1 Samuel 16:7). Justin Martyr cites the verse for Christ's first coming 'without form or honor' (Dialogue with Trypho 14, 49). The pagan critic Celsus mocked Jesus as small and ugly; Origen answered that Isaiah had foretold his lack of beauty, while the Psalms praise his beauty (Psalm 45:2) in another sense (Against Celsus 6.75–77).

a: He was despised, and people kept away from him
p: Chadal 'ishim may mean 'abandoned by people' or 'the lowest of men'.
b: Chadal means to stop, to leave off, to lack. Chadal 'ishim may be 'forsaken by people' (KJV 'rejected of men'), 'lacking in men' (without friends), or 'the least of men'. The Plain English Translation gives the sense that people kept their distance. The next lines may describe a sufferer from skin disease, whom people avoided and who had to cover his face (Leviticus 13:45), or someone so disfigured that onlookers hid their faces from him (52:14). 'We counted him as nothing' admits the speakers' own contempt.

a: a man of pains who knew sickness well
p: The Hebrew speaks of physical pains and sickness; the KJV's 'sorrows' and 'grief' make them sound like sadness.
b: Makh'ovot are pains, both of body and of heart (Exodus 3:7; Job 33:19), and choli is sickness, the ordinary word for illness (1 Kings 17:17; 38:9). The KJV's "a man of sorrows, and acquainted with grief", made famous by Handel's Messiah, follows the Latin virum dolorum et scientem infirmitatem and leans toward sadness. The Plain English Translation keeps the physical sense, which Matthew follows when he applies 53:4 to Jesus's healings (Matthew 8:17). 'The Man of Sorrows' became a subject of late medieval art: Christ standing with his wounds.
orig: איש מכאבות וידוע חלי ('ish makh'ovot viydua' choli)

a: Yet it was our sicknesses that he carried
p: Matthew applies this line to Jesus's healings; 1 Peter applies the next verses to his death for sins.
b: 'Akhen, 'yet surely', marks the turning point of the confession: the sicknesses and pains were ours, not his. Matthew, after a day of healings, says this happened "so that what was spoken through Isaiah the prophet would be fulfilled: 'He himself took our weaknesses and carried our diseases'" (Matthew 8:17). His wording follows the Hebrew; the Greek has 'he bears our sins'. 1 Peter 2:24 instead speaks of Christ bearing 'our sins in his body on the tree'. Whether healing of the body is promised in the atonement is a question the churches answer differently; see the card on this page.

a: But we thought of him as stricken
t: "The leper of the house of Rabbi"
p: The Talmud names the Messiah from this verse, showing that rabbis too read the chapter of the Messiah.
b: The onlookers thought the servant's suffering proved God was punishing him for his own sins, the reasoning of Job's friends. Nagua', 'stricken', is used of a person struck with skin disease (2 Kings 15:5; Leviticus 13). In the Babylonian Talmud (Sanhedrin 98b), rabbis give the Messiah's name, and "the Rabbis say: the leper of the house of Rabbi is his name", citing this verse. Ruth Rabbah 5:6 also applies the sufferings of 53:5 to the Messiah. These texts show that a messianic reading of the chapter existed in rabbinic Judaism alongside the reading of it as Israel.

a: But he was pierced because of our rebellions
p: Mecholal means 'pierced, wounded'; the Targum reads a word of the same root as 'profaned' and applies it to the Temple.
b: Mecholal comes from chalal, 'to pierce, wound', as in 51:9 ("ran the dragon through") and of those 'slain' in battle. A second root chalal means 'to profane'. The Targum reads the verse: the Messiah 'will build the sanctuary which was profaned for our sins, handed over for our iniquities'. That reading moves the suffering from a person to the Temple. 'Because of our rebellions' (mippesha'enu, literally 'from our rebellions') means 'on account of' them: the servant was wounded on account of other people's sins. The KJV's 'wounded for our transgressions' is close to the Hebrew.

a: The discipline that bought our peace lay on him
t: The punishment that brought us peace
p: Musar shelomenu is the discipline that won our well-being; the Plain English Translation keeps both words.
b: Musar is correction or discipline, by word or blow (Proverbs 3:11; 22:15), and shalom is wholeness and well-being. 'The discipline of our peace' (KJV 'the chastisement of our peace') means the correction that resulted in our well-being fell on him instead of us. The verse is one of the strongest bases for the doctrine that the servant suffered in the place of others. Christian traditions explain that substitution in different ways, and Jewish interpreters read it as Israel suffering for the nations or the righteous for the wicked; see the card on this page.

a: and by his welts healing came to us
p: Chavurah is a welt or stripe left by a lash; 1 Peter quotes the line to suffering slaves.
b: Chavurah is a bruise or welt, the mark left by a whip (Exodus 21:25; Proverbs 20:30). The KJV's 'with his stripes we are healed' is literal. 1 Peter 2:24 quotes the Greek, 'by his wound you were healed', in a passage addressed to household slaves who suffer unjustly: Christ's suffering is both their example and their healing (1 Peter 2:18–25). 'Healing' in Isaiah often means the restoration of a sick nation (1:5–6; 6:10; 30:26; 57:18–19). Pentecostal and Word of Faith teachers read it also as a promise of bodily healing; see the card on this page.

a: We had all strayed like sheep
p: 1 Peter applies the line to believers who have returned to their shepherd.
