b: The confession widens: not only did 'we' misjudge the servant, 'we' all went our own way like lost sheep (Psalm 119:176; Jeremiah 50:6; Ezekiel 34:5–6). 1 Peter 2:25 completes its quotation of 53 with this line: 'For you were straying like sheep, but now you have turned back to the shepherd and overseer of your souls.' Jesus's parable of the lost sheep (Luke 15:4–7; Matthew 18:12–14) uses the same picture. The lamb of 53:7 is himself among the flock.
r: 1 Peter 2:25; Psalm 119:176; Ezekiel 34:5–6; Jeremiah 50:6; Luke 15:4–7; Matthew 18:12–14

a: and the LORD made the guilt of us all
p: Hifgia' means 'caused to strike'; the same verb ends the passage as 'he will step in' (53:12).
b: Hifgia' bo means 'made (it) meet him, strike him'; the guilt of all 'lands on' the servant like a blow. In 53:12 the same verb appears again: yafgia', 'he will intercede, step in' for the rebels. The guilt that struck him and his pleading for the guilty are expressed by one word. Leviticus 16:21–22 describes the goat that carries 'all their guilty deeds on itself to a land cut off'; compare 53:8, 'cut off from the land of the living'. The Greek has 'the Lord handed him over to our sins', the verb Paul uses in Romans 4:25.

a: yet he did not open his mouth
p: The servant's silence is echoed in the Gospels' account of Jesus before the high priest and Pilate.
b: Niggas is the word for a taskmaster driving slaves (Exodus 3:7; 5:6), and na'aneh 'he let himself be afflicted' or 'he humbled himself'. Unlike Jeremiah, who cried out for vengeance (Jeremiah 11:20), the servant does not protest. Matthew records that at his trial "Jesus stayed silent" (Matthew 26:63), "he answered nothing" (Matthew 27:12), and "did not reply to him with even one word, and the governor was very surprised" (Matthew 27:14). 1 Peter 2:23 draws the lesson: 'when he was insulted, he did not insult in return.'
r: Matthew 26:62–63; Matthew 27:12–14; Mark 14:61; Mark 15:5; 1 Peter 2:23; Jeremiah 11:20; Exodus 3:7

a: Like a lamb that is taken off to slaughter
p: The Ethiopian official reads this verse in his chariot, and Philip tells him about Jesus.
b: In Acts 8:26–35 an Ethiopian court official, returning from worship in Jerusalem, is reading aloud from Isaiah: 'Like a sheep he was led to slaughter, and like a lamb silent before its shearer, so he does not open his mouth...' (Acts 8:32–33, quoting the Greek). He asks, 'About whom does the prophet say this, about himself or about someone else?', the very question this passage still raises. Philip, 'starting from this Scripture', tells him the good news about Jesus. Jeremiah used the image of himself: 'like a gentle lamb led to the slaughter' (Jeremiah 11:19); Saadia Gaon (as Ibn Ezra reports) and, centuries later, Hugo Grotius identified the servant with Jeremiah. John the Baptist calls Jesus "the Lamb of God", "the one who takes the world's sin away" (John 1:29), and Revelation's "Lamb ... as though he had been slaughtered" (Revelation 5:6) carries the same picture.
r: Acts 8:26–35; Jeremiah 11:19; John 1:29; Revelation 5:6; 1 Peter 1:19; Psalm 44:22

a: Through arrest and sentence he was taken off
p: The Hebrew is compressed; the Greek, quoted in Acts, reads differently.
b: Me'otser umimmishpat luqqach: 'from restraint and from judgment he was taken'. Most read it as an unjust arrest and trial that led to his death; some read 'he was taken away from' (rescued from) prison and judgment. The KJV has 'He was taken from prison and from judgment'. The Greek, quoted in Acts 8:33, reads 'In his humiliation his judgment was taken away', that is, he was denied justice. 'Taken' (luqqach) is the word used of Enoch and Elijah taken by God (Genesis 5:24; 2 Kings 2:10), which some find suggestive.

a: and as for his generation, who gave it a thought?
p: Dor means 'generation'; the Greek and KJV make it a question about his origin or descendants.
b: Ve'et-doro mi yesocheach is literally 'and his generation, who considers?'. Most modern scholars take it as 'who among his contemporaries cared?' or 'who thought about his fate?'. The Greek, quoted in Acts 8:33, has 'Who will describe his generation?', and the KJV follows: 'who shall declare his generation?'. Church fathers such as Justin read it of the mystery of Christ's origin, his eternal begetting or his birth from a virgin (Dialogue with Trypho 43, 63). Others took 'generation' as his descendants: he died childless, yet 'will see offspring' (53:10).
orig: ואת דורו מי ישוחח (ve'et-doro mi yesocheach)

a: he was cut off from the land of the living
p: The words are those used of death; readers who take the servant as Israel hear exile as a kind of death.
b: Nigzar me'erets chayyim, 'cut off from the land of the living', is the language of death (Psalm 88:5; Lamentations 3:54; Jeremiah 11:19, "let us cut him off from the land of the living"), and 53:9 speaks of his grave. The Christian reading takes it as a real death followed by vindication (53:10–12), which the New Testament sees in Jesus's death and resurrection. Jewish interpreters who read the servant as Israel point to Ezekiel 37, where exiled Israel is a valley of dry bones, dead and buried, then raised: exile is national death, and return is resurrection. On either reading, the servant's life continues after it (53:10).

a: the blow fell on him
p: Lamo usually means 'to them'; Jewish interpreters cite it as evidence that the servant is a people.
b: Nega' lamo: 'a blow (was) to them' or 'to him'. Lamo is normally plural, and Jewish writers, among them Isaac of Troki in Faith Strengthened (about 1594), pointed to it as evidence that the servant stands for a group, the people Israel. Christian scholars answer that lamo is sometimes singular in poetry (as perhaps 44:15, 'he bows down to it'), and the Greek reads 'he was led to death'. Origen, debating a Jewish reading in his own day, argued from 'my people' in the same line: if Israel is the people for whose sins the servant suffers, the servant cannot be Israel (Against Celsus 1.55). Jewish interpreters answer that 'my people' is spoken by the nations' kings, each of his own nation (Rashi), so that it does not name Israel as the beneficiary; and 1QIsa-a and 1QIsa-b read 'his people' (see the variant on this verse).

a: They gave him a burial place among the wicked
t: With the wicked and the rich
p: Jesus died between two bandits and was buried in a rich man's tomb.
b: The Hebrew is literally 'he (one) gave his grave with the wicked, and with a rich man in his deaths'. Poetic parallelism suggests 'rich' stands beside 'wicked' as another word for oppressors (as in Micah 6:12; James 5:1–6), and some scholars emend 'ashir, 'rich', to 'ose ra', 'evildoers'. The Gospels tell that "two bandits were crucified alongside him" (Matthew 27:38) and that "a rich man from Arimathea" (Matthew 27:57) laid the body in his own new tomb, "carved out of the rock" (Matthew 27:60). Christians since the early church have seen both lines fulfilled, while the Gospels themselves do not cite the verse.

a: in his deaths
p: The Hebrew noun is plural; the Plain English Translation keeps the plural so that the debate stays visible.
b: Bemotav is plural, 'in his deaths'. Some take it as an intensive or abstract plural, 'his death, his violent death' (compare the plural in Ezekiel 28:10, "the death of the uncircumcised," which the Plain English Translation gives as a singular). Others hear a true plural: the many deaths of a people that dies and is raised again in each exile, which is how Ibn Ezra and Isaac of Troki use the word to support the reading of the servant as Israel. The scrolls differ in spelling here (see the variant). The Plain English Translation keeps the plural, 'deaths', so the reader can weigh it.

a: even though he never did violence
p: 1 Peter applies the line to Christ; Zephaniah uses similar words of the faithful remnant.
b: The servant suffered although he was innocent. 1 Peter 2:22 quotes the Greek: 'He committed no sin, and no deceit was found in his mouth' (the Greek has 'lawlessness' for 'violence'; Peter has 'sin'). Zephaniah 3:13 says of the humble remnant of Israel that "A tongue of deceit will not be found in their mouths", and Revelation 14:5 says of the 144,000, "Not one lie was found in their mouths". Interpreters who read the servant as Israel point to Zephaniah; those who read Jesus point to 1 Peter.

a: But the LORD desired to crush him
p: The Talmud reads this verse of the righteous whom God tests through suffering, if they accept it in love.
b: Chafets dakke'o, 'he desired to crush him', is the boldest line of the song: the servant's suffering was God's will. In the Babylonian Talmud (Berakhot 5a), Rava says in the name of Rav Sechora, in the name of Rav Huna: 'Anyone in whom the Holy One delights, he crushes with sufferings', citing this verse; and if the sufferer accepts them in love ('if his life is made a guilt offering'), 'he will see offspring and lengthen his days'. These are the 'sufferings of love' (yissurin shel ahavah). The New Testament speaks in a similar way of God's set purpose in Jesus's death (Acts 2:23; 4:27–28) and adds that his suffering was for others.

a: If his life is made a guilt offering
p: The asham was the offering of reparation; the subject of the verb is uncertain.
b: The asham, 'guilt offering' or 'reparation offering', was brought when someone had wronged God or a neighbor and owed compensation (Leviticus 5:14–6:7; 7:1–7); a flawless ram was its usual animal (Leviticus 5:15). Here the servant's own life is the offering. The verb tasim is, as the Hebrew stands, either 'you make' (second person) or 'she makes' (third person feminine, with nafsho, 'his life', as the subject: 'if his life makes a guilt offering'); a small change would give 'he makes'. The Plain English Translation follows the third-person feminine reading, in a passive form ('if his life is made a guilt offering'), and does not follow the emendation. The Greek has 'if you give an offering for sin'. Jesus says the Son of Man came "to give his life as a ransom in place of many" (Matthew 20:28; Mark 10:45), which many scholars hear as an echo of 53:10–12, though others, such as Morna Hooker, doubt a direct link.
orig: אם תשים אשם נפשו ('im tasim 'asham nafsho)
r: Leviticus 5:14–19; Leviticus 7:1–7; Matthew 20:28; Mark 10:45; Hebrews 10:10; 1 Samuel 6:3

a: he will see offspring; he will lengthen his days
p: Promises of children and long days seem to Jewish readers to fit a people, not a man who died.
b: Yir'eh zera', 'he will see seed', is the ordinary language of descendants, and 'lengthening days' is long life (Deuteronomy 5:33; Psalm 91:16). Jewish interpreters, among them Abravanel, argued that these blessings suit the people Israel, which survives exile and multiplies (54:1–3), better than a single martyr. Christian readers take them as life after death: the servant, cut off and buried (53:8–9), lives again and sees spiritual children (compare Hebrews 2:10–13; John 12:24). Either way, the song insists that death is not the end of the servant's story.

a: By his knowledge my servant, the righteous one, will put the many in the right
t: "He will put the many in the right"
p: The servant puts many in the right; Daniel 12:3 and Paul's 'the many will be made righteous' echo the line.
b: Yatsdiq tsaddiq 'avdi larabbim: 'the righteous one, my servant, will justify the many'. The Plain English Translation uses one rendering, 'put in the right', for this Hiphil verb here and in 50:8, where it is plainly a court word ("the one who puts me in the right"). The Hebrew order is 'the righteous one, my servant'; the Plain English Translation moves it for English. The Vulgate has iustificabit, and Catholic teachers read the verb as 'make righteous' in the sense of changing a person (Council of Trent, session 6); Lutheran and Reformed teachers read the court sense, being declared and counted righteous (Romans 4:25; 5:19). The verb alone does not settle that old dispute, and the Plain English Translation tries not to settle it by its wording. 'By his knowledge' may mean by knowing God, by his insight (52:13), or by others' knowledge of him. 'The many' (harabbim) recurs five times in 52:13–53:12. The earliest reuse of this line inside the Bible is Daniel 12:3, where the wise 'make many righteous' (matsdiqe harabbim). Paul writes that 'through the obedience of the one, the many will be made righteous' (Romans 5:19) and that Jesus 'was handed over for our trespasses and raised for our justification' (Romans 4:25). At Qumran, 'the Many' was a name for the community's full members.
orig: יצדיק צדיק עבדי לרבים (yatsdiq tsaddiq 'avdi larabbim)

a: and he himself will carry their guilt
p: The verb is the one used of God carrying Israel in 46:4.
b: Yisbol, 'he will carry (as a load)', is the verb used in 46:4: "I am the one who will carry you". The God who carries Israel has a servant who carries their guilt. Lamentations 5:7 uses it of children carrying their parents' guilt. Hebrews 9:28 says Christ was offered once 'to bear the sins of many', and 1 Peter 2:24 that he 'bore our sins in his body'.

a: So I will give him his share with the many
p: The servant receives the victor's portion; the Greek has 'he will inherit many'.
b: Achalleq lo varabbim may mean 'I will give him a share among the many (the great)' or 'I will give him the many as his share'. The second line, 'he will split the spoil with the mighty', is a picture of a victorious general. The Greek has 'he will inherit many'. The 'therefore' (lakhen) is the hinge of the song: because he gave himself, he is exalted. Philippians 2:9 follows the same pattern after describing Christ's self-emptying 'to the point of death': 'Therefore God also highly exalted him.'

a: because he emptied out his life to the point of death
t: Moses who poured out his soul
p: The Talmud reads this verse of Moses, who offered his life for Israel after the golden calf.
b: He'erah lammavet nafsho, 'he laid bare, poured out his life to death'. In the Babylonian Talmud (Sotah 14a), Rabbi Simlai applies the verse to Moses: he 'poured out his soul to death', for he said, "wipe me out, please, from your book" (Exodus 32:32); he 'was counted with the rebels', for he died in the wilderness with the generation that sinned; he 'bore the sin of many', for he won atonement for the golden calf; and he 'stepped in for the rebels', for he prayed for them. Many Christian scholars hear Philippians 2:7–8 ('he emptied himself... becoming obedient to the point of death') against this verse.

a: and was counted with the rebels
p: Jesus quotes this line on the night of his arrest.
b: In Luke 22:37 Jesus says at the Last Supper: 'This Scripture must be fulfilled in me: "And he was counted with the lawless"', the only place in the Gospels where he quotes Isaiah 53 directly. Some later manuscripts of Mark add the same quotation after the crucifixion between two bandits (Mark 15:28, in the KJV but not in most modern versions). On the Moses reading of the line, see the note on 'emptied out his life'.

a: He bore the sin of many
p: Jesus's words at the Last Supper about blood 'poured out for many' echo the servant's death for 'the many'.
b: 'The many' are the servant's beneficiaries throughout the song (52:14–15; 53:11–12). At the Last Supper Jesus says, "For this is my blood of the covenant. It is being poured out for many, so that sins can be forgiven" (Matthew 26:28; compare Mark 14:24), and earlier, that the Son of Man came "to give his life as a ransom in place of many" (Matthew 20:28). Hebrews 9:28 says Christ was offered once 'to bear the sins of many'. The Great Isaiah Scroll and 4QIsa-d have the plural 'sins of many'; see the variant.
r: Matthew 26:28; Matthew 20:28; Mark 10:45; Mark 14:24; Hebrews 9:28; 1 Peter 2:24

a: and he will step in for the rebels
p: Yafgia' is to intervene or plead; the same verb in 53:6 describes guilt striking him.
b: Yafgia' means to meet, to step between, to plead on someone's behalf (Jeremiah 7:16; 15:11). It is the same verb as 'made fall on' in 53:6: the servant on whom the guilt struck steps in for the guilty. The Targum says that 'for his sake the rebellious will be forgiven'. The Greek reads 'because of their iniquities he was handed over'. Christians have seen fulfillment in Jesus's prayer from the cross, 'Father, forgive them' (Luke 23:34), and in his continuing intercession (Romans 8:34; Hebrews 7:25).

a: Sing for joy, you barren one who has borne no child!
p: Paul quotes this verse in Galatians 4 for the 'Jerusalem above', the mother of believers.
b: After the servant's death and vindication, Zion is told to sing: the barren city will have more children than ever. The verse opens the fifth synagogue reading of consolation (54:1–10, for the Sabbath of Ki Tetse). In Galatians 4:27 Paul quotes it word for word from the Greek ('Rejoice, barren one who does not give birth; break out and shout, you who are not in labor, because the children of the desolate one are more than those of the one who has the husband'). He reads Sarah, once barren, as the free 'Jerusalem above', and Hagar as the present Jerusalem (Galatians 4:21–31). 2 Clement 2 applies the verse to the church of the Gentiles.

a: Widen the space of your tent
p: William Carey's sermon on these verses in 1792 helped launch the modern Protestant missionary movement.
b: Zion is pictured as a tent-dwelling mother like Sarah, who must lengthen the ropes and drive the pegs deeper for a growing family. On 31 May 1792, at a meeting of Baptist ministers in Nottingham, England, William Carey preached on 54:2–3 with the call usually remembered as 'Expect great things from God; attempt great things for God'. Within months the Baptist Missionary Society was formed, and Carey sailed for India in 1793. His reading applies Zion's growth to the church among the nations.

a: your offspring will drive out nations
p: The promise repeats the words given to Jacob at Bethel.
b: 'You will spread out (tifrotsi) to the right and to the left' takes up God's promise to Jacob: "you will break out westward and eastward, northward and southward" (Genesis 28:14). 'Drive out nations' (goyim yirash) uses the conquest word of Deuteronomy (Deuteronomy 9:1; 11:23). Some take it as possessing the lands of nations, some as gaining nations as a possession; the next line has the deserted cities filled again.

a: the insults of your widowhood
p: Zion's early shame and her 'widowhood' in exile will both be forgotten.
b: 'The shame of your youth' may be Israel's slavery in Egypt or its early unfaithfulness (Jeremiah 3:24–25; Ezekiel 16:22); 'widowhood' is the exile, when Zion seemed bereft of her husband. Lamentations begins: 'How she has become like a widow' (Lamentations 1:1). Babylon boasted that she would never be a widow (47:8); now Zion's widowhood ends.

a: For your husband is your Maker
p: The marriage image of Hosea, Jeremiah and Ezekiel returns: Zion's husband is her Creator.
b: The Hebrew uses plural forms for 'your husband' and 'your maker' (bo'alayikh 'osayikh), a plural of majesty. The prophets often picture the covenant as a marriage broken by Israel's unfaithfulness (Hosea 2; Jeremiah 2–3; Ezekiel 16). Here the husband takes back the wife he sent away for a moment (54:6–7; compare 50:1). He is also 'the God of the whole earth', so his bride's restoration concerns all nations. The New Testament takes up the image for Christ and the church (Ephesians 5:25–32; Revelation 21:2, 9).

a: When my anger overflowed
t: A flood of anger, a lifetime of love
p: Shetsef qetsef, 'a flood of anger', is a rhyme; the moment of anger is set against love that never ends.
b: Beshetsef qetsef rhymes: 'in a surge of fury'. The contrast is between a 'moment' (rega', 54:7–8) and 'a loyal love that never ends' (chesed 'olam). Psalm 30:5 says the same: "His anger is over in a moment; his favor is for life." 'I hid my face' is the language of God's withdrawal in exile (Deuteronomy 31:17–18; 8:17; 45:15). Paul's 'momentary light affliction' and 'eternal weight of glory' (2 Corinthians 4:17) may echo the contrast.

a: To me this is like the waters of Noah
p: As God swore never again to flood the earth, he swears not to be angry with Zion again.
b: After the flood God promised: "there will not again be a flood to ruin the earth" (Genesis 9:11; compare Genesis 8:21; Genesis 9:15). The exile was Zion's flood; God's new oath is as firm as the covenant with Noah and the rainbow. Many Hebrew manuscripts and the Latin read 'like the days of Noah' for 'the waters of Noah'; see the variant. Jesus compares the coming of the Son of Man to 'the days of Noah' (Matthew 24:37), and 1 Peter 3:20–21 links Noah's waters with baptism.

a: and my covenant of peace will not be shaken
p: Mountains may move, but God's loyal love will not; Ezekiel promises the same covenant.
b: The 'covenant of peace' (berit shelomi) was given to Phinehas ("I am giving him my covenant: peace", Numbers 25:12), and Ezekiel promises it to restored Israel (Ezekiel 34:25; 37:26). The mountains, the most stable things on earth, may 'move away' (the same verb as in the next line: God's love will not 'move away'). Psalm 46:2 uses the picture of mountains slipping into the sea. Paul's 'love never fails' and 'neither height nor depth' (Romans 8:38–39) have the same confidence.

a: look, I will set your stones in dark mortar
p: The names of the stones are uncertain; the picture is a city built entirely of precious materials.
b: Puk is antimony, the dark powder used as eye paint (2 Kings 9:30; Jeremiah 4:30): here a dark mortar that sets off the stones. Sappirim are probably lapis lazuli, the deep blue stone with gold flecks prized in Mesopotamia; true sapphire was little known. Kadkod (54:12, 'rubies') and 'eqdach ('sparkling stones') are rare words, guessed as ruby, agate or carbuncle. The Greek has 'carbuncle', 'sapphire' and 'jasper'. Tobit 13:16 and Revelation 21:18–21 build their visions of the new Jerusalem from these verses: "The foundations of the city wall were decked with precious stones of every kind" (Revelation 21:19). A Qumran commentary (4Q164) reads the stones as the community's priests and leaders.

a: All your children will be the LORD's learners
p: Jesus quotes the line in John 6; the rabbis read 'your children' as 'your builders'.
b: Limmude YHWH are 'those taught by the LORD', the same word as the servant's 'learner's tongue' (50:4): Zion's children will be disciples like the servant. Jesus quotes it: "In the Prophets it is written: 'And all of them will be taught by God.' Anyone who has listened to the Father and learned from him comes to me" (John 6:45). Paul calls the Thessalonians 'God-taught' (1 Thessalonians 4:9), and Jeremiah 31:34 promises that all will know the LORD. In the Talmud (Berakhot 64a), Rabbi Elazar says Torah scholars increase peace in the world, citing this verse: 'Do not read banayikh, your children, but bonayikh, your builders.' The saying is recited in the daily prayers. The Great Isaiah Scroll in fact writes 'your builders' in the second half; see the variant.

a: If anyone stirs up trouble, it is not from me
p: The verb gur can mean 'stir up strife' or 'live as a foreigner'; the Greek speaks of proselytes.
b: The Plain English Translation reads gor yagur as 'stir up (attack)', as in Psalm 59:3: anyone who attacks Zion does so without God's sending and will fall. The same letters can mean 'to live as a resident foreigner', and the Greek took it that way: 'Look, proselytes will come to you through me, and will live beside you and flee to you for refuge.' The Greek translator, working in Egypt where Jews welcomed converts, read the verse as a promise that foreigners would join Israel.

a: and I created the destroyer to ruin
p: God made both the weapon-maker and the destroyer, so no weapon can act against his will.
b: The thought repeats 45:7 ("I make peace and create disaster"): both the craftsman who forges weapons and the destroyer who uses them are God's creatures. If God made them, they cannot defeat the people he protects (54:17). Compare Assyria as the axe in God's hand (10:15).

a: the LORD's servants
t: From the servant to the servants
p: After 53 the word 'servant' is always plural: the servant's 'offspring' (53:10) become the servants.
b: Up to 53:11 Isaiah speaks of 'my servant'. From 54:17 on, the book speaks only of 'servants' (56:6; 63:17; 65:8–15; 66:14). Many scholars see a deliberate link: the offspring the servant 'will see' (53:10) are the faithful who share his calling and his vindication. Readers who take the servant as an individual see his followers here; readers who take him as Israel see the faithful within Israel. The 'inheritance' (nachalah) recalls the land given to the tribes, now given to those who serve the LORD.

a: No weapon made against you will succeed
p: Tsedaqah here means the right God secures for his servants, their vindication.
b: The courtroom image is plain: every accusing tongue will be proved wrong. In the last line tsidqatam, 'their righteousness', is the verdict in their favor, the right God secures for them, so the Plain English Translation says 'vindication' (see 45:8). The verse is popular as a promise of protection; in context it promises that no accuser of Zion's servants will win their case before God (compare 50:8–9; Romans 8:33–34).

a: Hey! All you who are thirsty, come to the water!
p: A street-seller's cry offers water, wine and milk for nothing; Jesus and Revelation repeat the invitation.
b: Hoy, usually 'woe', is here a call to attention, like a vendor in the market. But the goods are free. Wisdom calls in the same way: "Come, have some of my bread, and drink the wine I mixed" (Proverbs 9:5), and Sirach 24:19–21 and 51:23–25 have Wisdom inviting the hungry. Jesus cries out at the Festival of Booths: "If anyone is thirsty, he should come to me and drink" (John 7:37). Revelation ends: "Let the one who is thirsty come. Let anyone who wants to take the water of life as a free gift" (Revelation 22:17; compare Revelation 21:6). In the synagogue, 54:11–55:5 is read as the third haftarah of consolation, for Re'eh.
r: Proverbs 9:1–6; Sirach 24:19–21; John 7:37–38; John 4:10–14; Revelation 21:6; Revelation 22:17; 44:3

a: Why pay out silver for something that is not bread
p: The bread and the rich food stand for God's word and life; Jesus speaks of food that lasts.
b: The exiles in Babylon may have been doing well in trade (compare 47:15); the prophet asks why they spend their lives on what does not satisfy. 'Listen... and eat' turns hearing God's word into a meal, as in Deuteronomy 8:3 ("people do not live by bread alone") and Amos 8:11. Jesus says: "Do not work for food that goes bad. Work for the food that remains, leading to eternal life" (John 6:27).
r: Deuteronomy 8:3; Amos 8:11; John 6:27; John 6:35; Matthew 4:4; Psalm 63:5

a: the sure loyal love of David
p: God's lasting love for David is now offered to all the people; Paul quotes the Greek in Acts 13.
b: Chasde David hanne'emanim is 'the faithful acts of loyal love (promised to) David': God's oath that his loyal love would never leave David's line (2 Samuel 7:15–16; Psalm 89:28, "For all time I will guard my loyal love toward him"; Psalm 89:49). Here the covenant is made 'with you', plural: the promise to the king is extended to the whole people, a reading many scholars favor (Westermann; compare 55:4–5). Others hear a renewed Davidic king (Jeremiah 30:9; Ezekiel 34:23–24). The Greek has 'the holy things of David, the faithful ones', and in Acts 13:34–37 Paul quotes it beside Psalm 16:10 to argue that God's promise to David is kept in Jesus, raised never to die again. The KJV's 'the sure mercies of David' is a well-known phrase.
r: 2 Samuel 7:15–16; Psalm 89:28; Psalm 89:49; Acts 13:34–37; Psalm 16:10; Jeremiah 30:9; Ezekiel 34:23–24; 2 Chronicles 6:42

a: Look, I made him a witness to the peoples
p: David is a witness to the nations; now Israel will call nations it does not know.
b: 'Him' is David, whose victories made him 'chief over the nations' (Psalm 18:43, "A people I never knew serve me"). As David's rule showed the nations who the LORD is, so now Israel ('you', 55:5) will call a nation it does not know, and they will run to it. Readers who see a coming Davidic ruler in 55:3 hear the Messiah as 'witness' and 'leader'; Revelation 1:5 calls Jesus 'the faithful witness' and 'ruler of the kings of the earth'.

a: Look for the LORD while he lets himself be found
p: The call to seek the LORD is the synagogue reading for the afternoon of public fast days.
b: The verse is the reason for repentance (55:7): God can be found now, while he is near (Deuteronomy 4:29, "you will search for the LORD your God, and you will find him"; Jeremiah 29:13–14; Amos 5:4–6). In the synagogue, 55:6–56:8 is the haftarah read at the afternoon service on public fast days, including the Ninth of Av, in the Ashkenazi rite. The Talmud discusses when God is 'near', applying it to the ten days between the New Year and the Day of Atonement (Rosh Hashanah 18a).

a: to our God, who forgives over and over
p: Yarbeh lisloach means 'he will multiply forgiveness'.
b: Yarbeh lisloach is 'he will do much forgiving' (KJV 'he will abundantly pardon'). The verb salach is used only of God's forgiveness in the Hebrew Bible. The invitation goes to 'the wicked man' and 'the man of trouble' ('ish 'aven): no one is beyond it. The following verses explain that God's thoughts of mercy are higher than human ones.

a: For my thoughts are not your thoughts
p: Often quoted for God's mystery in general; in context it means God forgives more than people would.
b: The verse is widely used to say that God's ways are beyond understanding (compare Romans 11:33–34, which quotes Isaiah 40:13). In context the 'for' ties it to 55:7: people would not forgive so freely, but God's thoughts and ways are as far above theirs as heaven is above earth, and so is his mercy (Psalm 103:11, "For like the height of the heavens over the earth, his loyal love stands strong over those who fear him"). The contrast is about grace, not only about mystery.

a: so will my word be that goes out from my mouth
t: The word that does not return empty
p: The book of comfort begins and ends with the word of God that stands and succeeds.
b: As rain does not go back to the sky until it has watered the earth, God's word does not come back to him 'empty' (reqam, the word for going home empty-handed) until it has done its work. Chapters 40–55 open with "our God's word will stand forever" (40:8) and close here. Paul echoes 55:10, 'seed to the sower and bread to eat', when he writes of God supplying generosity (2 Corinthians 9:10). Hebrews 4:12 calls God's word living and active, and Jesus's parable of the sower (Mark 4:3–20) pictures the same seed and harvest.

a: will clap its hands
p: All creation joins the new exodus with joy, as in the psalms of the LORD's kingship.
b: The exiles go out in joy (compare 52:12), and nature applauds: mountains sing, trees clap. Psalm 98:8 has "Let the rivers clap palm to palm", and Psalm 96:12 has the trees of the forest singing. The first exodus was a flight; the second is a festival procession. The line is the basis of the popular worship song 'You shall go out with joy'.

a: Instead of the thornbush, the cypress will grow
p: The curse of thorns is reversed, and the renewed land becomes a lasting sign of the LORD's name.
b: Thorns and briers mark the curse on the ground (Genesis 3:18, "Thorn and thistle it will sprout for you") and the judgment on the vineyard (5:6; 7:23–25). Now the cypress and the myrtle, trees of festival (Nehemiah 8:15) and of Zechariah's vision (Zechariah 1:8), grow in their place. The renewed land will be 'a sign forever', like the rainbow after the flood (Genesis 9:12–17; compare Isaiah 54:9). With this the book of comfort, chapters 40–55, closes.
